articles.title: Cold War memories stir Rubio in Iceland as he champions diplomacy and downplays differences - AP News
articles.summary: Cold War memories stir Rubio in Iceland as he champions diplomacy and downplays differences  AP NewsIn Iceland, Rubio Dodges a Diplomatic Flap Over a Trump Map  The New York TimesSecretary of State Marco Rubio And Icelandic Foreign Minister Þorgerður Katrín Gunnarsdóttir At a Joint Press Availability  U.S. Department of State (.gov)Rubio starts European tour in Iceland to boost security ties  Al JazeeraRubio begins three-nation NATO tour in Iceland, which ...
articles.full_text:
REYKJAVIK, Iceland (AP) — U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday sought to reassure NATO ally Iceland that President Donald Trump’s administration has no designs on the island but shares its deep concerns about Arctic security as tensions between the United States and Russia rise in the High North and elsewhere.
Rubio hailed the role of diplomacy in resolving conflicts as he began a three-nation tour of NATO allies in the capital of Iceland, where concerns over the Republican administration’s often brusque and sometimes rude approach to traditional friends and partners have stirred unease.
Rubio, whose stops also include Greece and Portugal, met Tuesday with Iceland’s minister for foreign affairs, Thorgerdur Katrín Gunnarsdóttir, at Reykjavik’s Hofdi House, the site of the 1986 summit between U.S. President Ronald Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev that is widely regarded as the beginning of the end of the Cold War.
“The house symbolizes diplomacy’s role in ending the Cold War and defeating communism,” Rubio posted on social media after the talks that took place just days before the 40th anniversary of the landmark meeting.
Both Rubio and Gunnarsdóttir downplayed differences and said both countries were committed to deepening and expanding military and commercial ties. Rubio made clear that the United States would not do anything in Iceland without Iceland’s consent.
“We would be open to having those conversations to see what we can do together,” he said, noting that the U.S. had a decades-long permanent military presence in Iceland until 2006, when shifting priorities caused it to close its Keflavik base outside of Reykjavik. He noted that priorities have shifted again.
And he went out of his way to praise Iceland: “We have tremendous respect for the people. We have respect for the country in the role it plays, and it has for a very long time,” he said.
Iceland’s foreign minister says she’s ‘focused on the future’
Iceland has been uneasy about Trump’s intentions toward it after he posted a map showing the colors of the U.S. flag sprawling across all of North America and extending to Iceland and Greenland. The wariness has persisted despite an agreement last month to increase the U.S. presence in the neighboring Danish territory of Greenland that appears to have ended Trump’s earlier demand for the U.S. to take full control.
But Tuesday, after Rubio’s talks with Gunnarsdóttir and Iceland Prime Minister Kristrún Frostadóttir, those tensions appeared to be on the wane.
Gunnarsdóttir said the matter had been largely, if not entirely, resolved. “We remain focused on the future,” she said.
Rubio, meanwhile, said he was not in Iceland to talk about social media posts. “Everything is very positive,” he said.
Rubio said Monday that the visit was intended to “advance our shared priorities: a secure Arctic, stronger commercial and energy ties, and closer defense cooperation.” He offered no hint of tensions with the island that, while a NATO member, has no standing army.
The map incident, however, alarmed Icelanders, and in response, Gunnarsdóttir summoned U.S. Ambassador Billy Long to a meeting at which she made it clear the post was unacceptable.
Iceland, which is just 180 miles (290 kilometers) from Greenland, had already been on edge after Trump mistakenly named the country four times while speaking about Greenland.
Thousands of Icelanders signed a petition urging the prime minister to reject Long before he took up his ambassador post in August after he made a crack this year about Iceland becoming the 52nd U.S. state and making him governor. He has since apologized for the quip.
US ambassador to Greece faces misconduct allegations
At Rubio’s next stop in Athens, he may be dealing with another ambassador controversy. Rep. Gregory Meeks, a New York Democrat who is the ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, has said he would investigate allegations of misconduct and impropriety by the U.S. ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle.
In a letter to Rubio, Meeks said that he wanted answers following the allegations reported by The Wall Street Journal last month and that he would call for Guilfoyle’s dismissal if the behavior outlined in the news report were true.
The Journal reported that Guilfoyle told guests at a reception that the U.S. could undermine the Greek government if it chose to, promoted the business interests of one particular Greek construction and energy company, and allowed its lobbyist into private diplomatic meetings.
Some Greek opposition parties have called for an inquiry into the allegations, but it’s unclear if they will proceed.
Guilfoyle, a former Fox News Channel host and California prosecutor who was once engaged to Trump’s son Donald Jr., has denied any wrongdoing, and Rubio has defended her before.
Guilfoyle, Rubio said after the Journal story appeared, “has been an incredible advocate for the president’s agenda in Greece and across Europe.” Rubio said he and Trump greatly value the ambassador’s “pivotal work and leadership,” notably on energy issues.
The Trump administration sees Greece as key to advancing the promotion and export of U.S.-produced liquefied natural gas to Southeastern and Central Europe.
Outside parliament on Tuesday, about 1,500 people gathered to protest Rubio’s visit and the war in Iran, chanting “American killers!”
The demonstration, organized by a communist labor union and other left-wing groups, was held ahead of extensive road closures planned in Athens on Wednesday.
Organizers said protests were held in at least 12 other Greek cities.
___
Associated Press writer Derek Gatopoulos in Athens contributed to this report.

articles.title: NATO readies drone‑AI strategy to swiftly defeat Russia in defensive war - CHOSUNBIZ - Chosunbiz
articles.summary: NATO readies drone‑AI strategy to swiftly defeat Russia in defensive war - CHOSUNBIZ  Chosunbiz
articles.full_text:
The North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) is drafting a new military strategy that combines new technologies such as drones and artificial intelligence (AI) with existing forces to prepare for a Russian attack. If Russia strikes NATO's eastern flank, the idea is to use low-cost drones and AI-based targeting to halt the advance, then destroy command-and-control systems to quickly rout Russian forces.
On the 5th (local time), Bloomberg said Alexis Grynkewich, NATO's Supreme Allied Commander Europe, is preparing a strategy document called the so-called "Theory of Victory" to win quickly against a Russian attack. Bloomberg said it directly reviewed the document, which is not classified.
Grynkewich plans to unveil the strategy on the 12th in Poland. The purpose is to present more clearly how NATO would respond if Russia violates NATO territory.
According to the document, if Russia attacks NATO territory, NATO would combine ground forces with capabilities under the "Eastern Flank Deterrence Initiative" to block the advance. This includes low-cost drones, systems operated by minimal personnel, and AI-based targeting. In particular, after securing conditions for NATO forces to operate freely, the goal is to quickly and overwhelmingly defeat Russian forces by destroying their command-and-control systems.
The strategy focuses on integrating new technologies that have grown important on the battlefield since Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine with NATO's existing weapons systems. NATO plans to show members how to operate legacy weapons and new capabilities together and to urge additional defense investment and preparedness.
As NATO members centered in Europe sharply increase defense spending, debate continues over whether to prioritize traditional weapons like tanks or the new technologies highlighted in the war in Ukraine. Bloomberg said the strategy aims to publicly demonstrate NATO's readiness while showing more concretely the military capabilities backed by higher defense budgets.
NATO emphasized that the strategy is for "defensive purposes." Col. Martin O'Donnell, Spokesperson for Commander Grynkewich, avoided commenting on specific plans but said, "NATO is purely defensive." He added, "The Supreme Allied Commander's theory of victory is simple: maintaining NATO's advantage," and, "Given the unstable and complex international security environment, we must now set the conditions to deter aggression and, if necessary, win if attacked."
The document also includes NATO's defensive character and the principle of avoiding unintended provocations. At the same time, it specifies that members must respond jointly to "hybrid threats," hostile acts that fall short of full-scale armed conflict. It explains that part of deterrence is showing sufficient response capability so the opponent judges it cannot win.
However, NATO does not currently see signs that Russia is preparing a conventional attack on the alliance. NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte recently said there are no signs Russia is preparing a conventional attack against NATO, but Europe should prepare for Russia's hybrid attacks that could persist over a long period.

BERLIN — Germany's foreign intelligence chief warned Monday of the rising risk of a direct clash with Russia as the Kremlin escalates its “shadow war” on Berlin and hits Ukraine with increasing brutality.
“Germany is in danger of being drawn into a violent conflict with Russia,” Martin Jäger, the head of the German’s foreign intelligence agency, or BND, told parliamentarians, citing what he called Russia’s attempted attack on a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane at Leipzig Airport in August as an example. “Germany has become a major obstacle to Russia’s hegemonic power projection in Europe and, as a result, a primary target of Russian actions.”
Jäger also warned that Russia’s invasion of Ukraine is entering its most dangerous phase yet as President Vladimir Putin faces growing domestic pressure to show military progress with the war entering its fifth winter.

articles.title: The New Red Sea Wars
articles.summary: Conflicts in the Middle East and the Horn of Africa have become inseparable.
articles.full_text:
On June 3, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio told the U.S. Congress that the fighting that had raged for three years in Sudan was now a “proxy war” and blamed Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) for frustrating American efforts to bring the conflict to an end. Rubio was saying out loud what many observers already knew: what started as a domestic power struggle has morphed into a wider regional war, drawing in outside powers and spilling across Sudan’s borders.
The spread of the conflict in Sudan is part of a larger geopolitical transformation. For much of the past century, policymakers have treated the Horn of Africa and the Arabian Peninsula as separate strategic regions divided by the Red Sea. That distinction is now evaporating. Wars on one side of the sea increasingly alter the military calculations on the other. This entanglement is only deepening in the wake of the United States’ and Israel’s decision in February to launch a war on Iran, driving a deeper wedge between Abu Dhabi and Riyadh (which were already at odds), weakening the American-anchored security order in the region, and underscoring the importance of securing the Red Sea for shipping.
For the past decade, the UAE has been the most aggressive outside player in the Horn of Africa, establishing ports and military bases, offering large financial packages to key allies, and involving itself extensively in Sudan’s civil war. But the recent war in Iran, along with the breakdown of the Emirati-Saudi security partnership in Yemen last December, made Riyadh less confident of Washington’s protection, more anxious about the UAE’s security ties to Israel, and more intent on controlling the Red Sea’s security picture. And so as Saudi Arabia has leaned into an alignment with Egypt, Turkey, and Pakistan, it has also brought that alignment to bear to strengthen key partnerships in the Horn. It is trying to counter factions in the Horn that are backed by the UAE or Israel even as it struggles to manage threats from Iran and its allies—including the Houthis, who have seized control of Yemen’s Red Sea coast.
At the same time, the risk of conflict is increasing between the Sudanese armed forces (SAF), backed by Saudi Arabia and its allies, and Ethiopia, an ally of the emirates, as well as the chance that another direct war could erupt between Ethiopia and Eritrea. A new war between Ethiopia and Eritrea on the Red Sea would likely turn into a regional conflict that overlaps with the one in Sudan. And it would not only be aggravated by the existing Emirati-Saudi rift—it might well deepen that divide.
Some Middle Eastern governments once saw the Horn of Africa as a low-stakes theater in which they could compete for leverage at relatively little cost. But as wars in the Middle East and the Horn become inextricably linked, a single security sphere is coalescing. Unless leaders in both the Middle East and the Horn recognize how interconnected their security dilemmas have become, instability will continue to ricochet in both directions, and the overlapping conflicts and disputes will become harder to resolve.
separation of powers
In some respects, the growing entanglement between the Horn of Africa and the Middle East is a return to a historical norm. Over millennia, the sea connected present-day Djibouti, Eritrea, Ethiopia, and Yemen, and people, goods, and cultural trends moved regularly among them. Amharic, Ethiopia’s dominant language, and Tigrinya, widely spoken in Eritrea and northern Ethiopia, are both Semitic tongues. Christianity spread early to what is now northern Ethiopia, making it home to one of the world’s oldest Christian Orthodox traditions.
In the sixth century, an Aksumite ruler based in modern-day Ethiopia briefly conquered parts of Yemen. Not long afterward, the Prophet Muhammad sent some of his earliest followers across the Red Sea to take refuge with a Christian Aksumite king there. Islam later spread across the sea and along Africa’s Indian Ocean coast. From the sixteenth to the twentieth century, the Ottoman Empire ruled territory on both sides of the Red Sea, and Omani rulers built an empire tying the Arabian Peninsula to much of East Africa’s coastline, eventually moving their capital from Muscat to Zanzibar. These links persisted into the modern age. When the Saudi kingdom conquered the Hejaz region on the western Arabian Peninsula in the early twentieth century, elites in the port city of Jeddah sent their families across the Red Sea to Port Sudan for safety. And in April 2023, when war erupted in Khartoum, many Sudanese took refuge in Jeddah.
Starting in the twentieth century, however, a separation began to harden between the two sides of the Red Sea as European colonialism and nationalist movements severed governance links crisscrossing the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden. Connections remained—for instance, Persian Gulf wealth flowed to nearby African countries and African labor and exports flowed the other way after a 1970s oil boom transformed the Gulf economies, and Middle East countries played a substantial role in a war during that decade between Ethiopia and Somalia. But the political gulf between the Arabian and African Red Sea shores widened further after the end of the Cold War. The first Gulf War, in 1990-91, upended the Middle East and expanded the U.S. military footprint there, giving Gulf states a reprieve from managing their near abroad. Around the same time, polities in the Horn began to fragment. Somalia’s collapse drove Somaliland, a former British colony along the Gulf of Aden, to claim independence in 1991. Regime change in Ethiopia led to the 1993 secession of Eritrea, and an intensified civil war in Sudan eventually prompted South Sudan’s 2011 secession.
The United States made fraught and often counterproductive efforts to try to manage these convulsions in the Horn of Africa. Yet it rarely saw the Horn and the Middle East, or its role in each region, as linked. While Gulf states focused on threats emanating from Iran and the Levant, the Horn turned inward.
Regional leaders in these areas also did not view them as intimately connected. East African leaders such as Ethiopian President Meles Zenawi primarily sought influence across the African continent rather than across the Red Sea, championing institutions such as the African Union. Influential Christian elites in both Ethiopia and Kenya, the Horn region’s two strongest countries, have little attachment to the Arab world. Political power in the Persian Gulf region was concentrated in Riyadh and around the Persian Gulf capitals of Abu Dhabi and Doha, not the Red Sea shore. When Sudan partitioned, the process was led by the African Union with backing from the United States and Europe; the Arab world was on the sidelines.
THE HORN CIRCLES BACK
During the turmoil of the Arab Spring, the Horn began to draw back into the Middle East’s sphere of influence. In a key turning point in 2011, Turkey’s Recep Tayyip Erdogan became the first non-African leader to visit Mogadishu, Somalia’s capital, in almost 20 years as he sought to expand Turkish influence in the region. The uprisings also destabilized Yemen and led to the Houthis’ takeover of much of the country in 2014. The decision by Saudi Arabia and the UAE to intervene militarily against the Houthis in 2015 increased the Horn’s strategic importance because Gulf states needed new military bases and personnel to sustain their campaign against the rebel group. The emirates opened a military base on the Eritrean coastline while Omar al-Bashir’s regime in Sudan sent tens of thousands of troops from the country’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces into Yemen to support the Saudi and Emirati efforts there.
At the same time, Middle Eastern countries had begun to doubt U.S. security commitments to the region amid the Obama administration’s widely publicized “pivot to Asia” and diplomacy with Iran, which accelerated their scramble to secure their own interests in a wider area. Middle Eastern governments became more anxious and competition among them grew more intense. A 2017 intra-Gulf crisis culminating in the blockade of Qatar by neighboring countries spilled directly into Africa, as loose blocs of patrons competed for influence and Saudi Arabia and the UAE pushed Horn leaders to choose a side. The UAE began to make increasingly ambitious political interventions in the Horn: for instance, it placed a major bet on the Ethiopian leader Abiy Ahmed, who rose to power in 2018, by backing his regime with an early infusion of $3 billion and providing critical military support when he faced a rebellion in the Tigray region.
The catastrophic war in Sudan further fused the Horn of Africa to the Middle East. When mass protests in 2019 threatened to topple Bashir’s regime in Khartoum, Abu Dhabi and Riyadh backed a military junta that seized power. After the junta’s two leaders turned on each other in 2023, the UAE emerged as the major patron of Sudan’s Rapid Support Forces, although Abu Dhabi formally denies the extent of its interventions. Saudi Arabia also had historic ties to the RSF and at first tried to mediate between the two sides, but the scope of the UAE’s intervention eventually led Riyadh to more firmly back the SAF. Saud Arabia has become the Sudanese army’s most important ally.
 Saudi Arabia has deepened its involvement in both Sudanese and Somali affairs.
Over the past year, those disputes in the Horn of Africa began to spill back across the Red Sea. Tensions between Abu Dhabi and Riyadh over the war in Sudan appeared to contribute to the breakup of the Emirati-Saudi partnership to counter the Houthis. In December 2025, Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government demanded that the UAE pull out of the country after a sudden offensive near the Saudi border by separatist forces backed by the emirates. articles.title: ICC opens investigation into Duterte drug war, DDS killings - Rappler
articles.summary: ICC opens investigation into Duterte drug war, DDS killings  Rappler
articles.full_text:
AT A GLANCE
- The International Criminal Court (ICC) has opened an investigation into the Philippine war on drugs, including killings by the Davao Death Squad.
- The investigation is a crucial stage where summons and arrest warrants can be issued if requested by the Prosecutor.
- President Duterte's administration remains firm in its stance that the ICC has no jurisdiction over the Philippines.
The International Criminal Court (ICC) pre-trial chamber has opened the crucial investigation into the Philippine war on drugs, the court’s pre-trial chamber announced on Wednesday, September 15.
“For these reasons, the chamber hereby authorizes the commencement of the investigation into the Situation in the Philippines, in relation to crimes within the jurisdiction of the Court allegedly committed on the territory of the Philippines between 1 November 2011 and 16 March 2019 in the context of the so-called ‘war on drugs’ campaign,” said the pre-trial chamber 1 of the ICC.
This means the ICC will look not only at President Rodrigo Duterte’s bloody war on drugs, but also at killings by the so-called Davao Death Squad when Duterte was mayor and vice mayor of Davao City.
The decision was signed by Presiding Judge Péter Kovács, Judge Reine Adélaïde Sophie Alapini-Gansou, and Judge María del Socorro Flores Liera.
The investigation is a crucial stage where summons and arrest warrants can be issued if Prosecutor Karim Khan asks for them.
“On the basis of the above, the Chamber concludes that there is a reasonable basis for the Prosecutor to proceed with an investigation, in the sense that the crime against humanity of murder appears to have been committed, and that potential case(s) arising from such investigation appear to fall within the Court’s jurisdiction,” said the judges.
Once again, the pre-trial chamber took into account Duterte’s statements, saying: “President Rodrigo Duterte has publicly encouraged extrajudicial killings in a way that is incompatible with a genuine law enforcement operation.”
Experts whom Rappler have talked to said that the Office of the Prosecutor (OTP) would like to take its time and tighten its case before requesting for summons and arrest warrants. Whoever the summons and arrest warrants are requested against will be assumed to be the ones who will be put on trial.
President Duterte’s chief legal counsel Salvador Panelo on Thursday, September 16, said the ICC chamber’s decision “neither bothers nor troubles the President and his administration.”
A pattern
It was newly-retired prosecutor Fatou Bensouda who asked the pre-trial chamber for authorization to open the investigation, which Malacañang persistently said would be denied, citing lack of jurisdiction.
In the decision, the pre-trial judges said Bensouda was able to sufficiently establish a pattern in the killings in Davao City when Duterte was mayor, up to the killings in the war on drugs when he was already president.
“In the assessment of the Chamber, there exists information sufficiently linking the killings in the Davao area in 2011-2016 to the relevant facts of the so-called ‘war on drugs’ campaign as discussed above,” said the pre-trial chamber.
The pre-trial chamber also said it would not be necessary at this stage to fully establish if the Davao City killings constitute crimes against humanity.
“What is important for the present decision is that, whichever the case may be, that it appears, on the basis of the supporting material, that the killings in the Davao area between 1 November 2011 and 30 June 2016 show a certain pattern and may constitute crimes against humanity within the jurisdiction of the Court,” said the pre-trial chamber.
Speaking for the Palace, Panelo said Malacañang stands firm on its stance that the ICC has no jurisdiction over the Philippines, claiming the Rome Statute which created the court “never took effect in the country” because it was never published on the Official Gazette.
However, lawyers’ groups have said such publication is not a requirement and that Republic Act 9851 or the Philippine Act on Crimes Against International Humanitarian Law, Genocide, and Other Crimes Against Humanity (International Humanitarian Law Act) allows “our courts to try cases cognizable by the ICC under the principle of complementarity.”
The pre-trial chamber also took note of the representations submitted by victims. The representation process was a stage where victims sent in their concerns and expectations without necessarily indicating they were willing to participate in court proceedings.
The judges said that representations also alleged other crimes apart from murder, like sexual violence.
“A legal analysis undertaken by the Registry has categorized the assertions and identified other inhumane acts/torture, imprisonment or other severe deprivation of liberty and enforced disappearance as the most commonly reported crimes other than murder. Moreover, the Chamber notes with particular attention that three representations reported sexual violence,” said the pre-trial judges.
Panelo insisted that the country’s justice system is able and willing to prosecute abusive law enforcers and officials “if only genuine complainants come forward to the proper authorities instead of personalities who will use their plight for political ambitions.”
He repeated the Malacañang accusation that the ICC is being politicized and used for “propaganda” by Duterte’s critics.
“While we expect that more theatrics will be employed by the detractors of the President as election season draws near, this blatant and brazen interference and assault on our sovereignty as an independent country by the ICC is condemnable,” said Panelo.
Malacañang has previously vowed never to cooperate with ICC investigators on any probe it will conduct on the drug war. – with reports from Pia Ranada/Rappler.com

articles.title: ‘Raging desire for revenge’: How does the Arab world remember Hamas’s October 7 invasion? - The Jerusalem Post
articles.summary: ‘Raging desire for revenge’: How does the Arab world remember Hamas’s October 7 invasion?  The Jerusalem PostIn Gaza, we cannot even begin to recover from trauma  Al JazeeraIsrael 'progressively asphyxiating' Gaza, continues genocide: Doctors Without Borders  Anadolu AjansıOctober 7: a Palestinian-Israeli memoir seeks to break the cycle of violence  The ConversationLive: Three years into the Palestine-Israel conflict  CGTN
articles.full_text:
Three years after Hamas's October 7 invasion of Israel, Arab media coverage of the anniversary has focused heavily on the devastation in Gaza, often making little or no mention of the Israeli civilians killed in the attack that sparked the war and sometimes going as far as to celebrate it.
The Jerusalem Post has not identified a statement from an Arab leader expressing sympathy for Israeli victims of the October 7 attack as of Tuesday. However, Hamas shared a condemnation of the statement issued by UN Secretary-General António Guterres on the invasion.
Hamas has continued to deny targeting civilians, carrying out sexual assaults and mistreating hostages in captivity, claiming that investigations had disproved the allegations. However, a UN mission that visited Israel concluded that there were reasonable grounds to believe conflict-related sexual violence occurred during the October 7 massacre and that there was clear and convincing information that hostages had been subjected to sexual violence in captivity.
Former hostages have also repeatedly described the torture, starvation, and sexual violence they experienced while they were held against their will in Gaza.
Hamas demanded Guterres retract his statement, which acknowledged Hamas and other Palestinian terrorists “brutally” killed more than 1,200 Israelis and foreign nationals, deliberately targeted civilians and sexually assaulted and tortured hostages in captivity.
Articles from the Arab world support 'Al-Aqsa Flood' massacre
Though Guterres expressed sympathy for the victims of October 7, his statement also addressed the “untold suffering on Palestinians in Gaza” and insisted that both Hamas and Israel need to enter the next stage of the ceasefire agreement.
The Egyptian state-owned Maspero marked the anniversary of Hamas’s October 7 attack using the terrorist group’s name for the assault, publishing an article titled “New details emerge about the Al-Aqsa Flood... and the region’s involvement in a chaos plot” that featured exclusively Palestinian and Egyptian professors.
The article failed to share the number of Israelis killed during the “crushing blow,” instead reporting only that Hamas was able to “occupy the settlements located in the envelope” and kill “hundreds of soldiers and officers of the Zionist entity.”
Unmentioned in the report was that more than 800 of those killed on October 7 were civilians. The youngest known victim was Naama Abu Rashed, a Bedouin-Israeli newborn who died just 14 hours after she was delivered by emergency Cesarean section after her pregnant mother was shot in the stomach while being driven to hospital.
“Events did not end with the clashes of October 7th. As expected, they escalated into a war of extermination waged by the Zionist entity against the Gaza Strip, during which approximately 74,000 Palestinians were killed, and about 100,000 others were wounded,” the report continued.
“Around 90 percent of Gaza's buildings were destroyed, and its infrastructure was almost completely obliterated. The war did not stop at Gaza; it extended to wars against Lebanon and then against Iran, leading to subsequent changes in the map of the Middle East.”
The state media did not mention Hezbollah’s attacks on October 8, 2023, which led to the war on the northern front, instead focusing on the view of Dr. Emad Mohsen, who alleged Israel “unleashed the killing machine accompanied by intense hatred, loathing, and a raging desire for revenge,” which resulted in “genocide, famine, crimes against humanity, and the most heinous forms of violent behavior on a human level.”
'Thirst for Palestinian and Arab blood... genocide, murder, displacement'
“Above all, the true face of Zionist extremism, its expansionist desire, its thirst for Palestinian and Arab blood, its call for displacement, genocide, murder, settlement, and the undermining of the Palestinian dream of freedom and national independence, was revealed,” the paper published.
Al Ghad, the first independent daily Arabic newspaper in Jordan, also failed to mention the specific number of victims in its article on the massacre, instead focusing on Israel closing the crossing from Gaza and the West Bank for two days.
“On the morning of October 7, 2023, Hamas surprised Israel with an unprecedented attack on 11 military bases and 22 settlements along the Gaza Strip, resulting in the death, injury, and capture of hundreds of Israelis,” it reported on Sunday, adding that the explanation that Hamas argued it committed the attack "to end the unjust siege on Gaza and to thwart Israel's plans to liquidate the Palestinian cause and impose its sovereignty over the Al-Aqsa Mosque."
It also focused on the civilian deaths in Gaza, relying on figures by the Hamas-run Gaza Health Ministry, which doesn’t distinguish between combatant and civilian deaths.
The independent Lebanese news website Janoubia published a practical analysis of the threats facing Israel and its military successes since October 7 in an article titled “8 dangers threatening Israel on ‘October 7th!’”
Although the article referred to the attack as “Operation Al-Aqsa Flood” and did not mention its victims, it focused on Israel’s security situation and acknowledged several of the IDF’s achievements. It also mentioned the displacement of Israelis from communities near the northern and southern borders following the attacks, an aspect of the war that has received relatively little attention in much international media coverage.
Asharq Al-Awsat, a Saudi-owned media group headquartered in London, published an article stressing that assassinated Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar had warned Israel in 2022 that Hamas would respond if Israel continued “attacks” on Al-Aqsa Mosque and Jerusalem.
The article attributed the launch of “Operation Al-Aqsa Flood” on October 7, 2023, to Israeli actions and focused on whether Hamas had achieved its objectives. It noted that Sinwar had promised to empty Israel’s prisons of security prisoners, thousands of whom were released as part of hostage-prisoner exchanges during the war.
The article also acknowledged Israel’s “unprecedented” success in assassinating Hamas’s leadership, while accusing the IDF of conducting “an indiscriminate bombing campaign across the Gaza Strip” and, citing a UN committee, claiming that “Israel has sought to wipe out Gaza through a genocide operation.”
At the same time, Asharq Al-Awsat quoted Gaza-based Palestinian political analyst Mustafa Ibrahim criticizing Sinwar, saying that “popular criticism of Sinwar and anger over his ill-considered decision continue,” alongside the suffering of Gaza residents who lost their homes and property. Bulgarian authorities on Tuesday launched a search for missing crew members of a boat that sank in its economic zone in the Black Sea after drones hit two merchant vessels. Black Sea shipping has been hit by growing fallout from the war in Ukraine in recent months.
Bulgarian authorities launched a major search on Tuesday for the missing crew of a ship that sank in the Black Sea after drones hit two vessels in what the prime minister slammed as an "absolutely unacceptable" attack.
The dual strike came a day after another ship caught fire and sank off the Romanian coast, killing one and leaving one missing, in what Ukraine said was a drone attack launched by Russia. Black Sea shipping has been hit by growing fallout from the Ukraine-Russia war in recent months.
A search operation was launched 70 nautical miles east of the coastal town of Byala, authorities said. The ship that sank was Togolese-flagged, according to the Maritime.bg specialised website.
The second ship, registered in Palau, was set alight by the drone but its Turkish and Indian crew members have been rescued.
A boat that rushed to the scene discovered overturned life rafts and life jackets near the ship that sank, but no members of the crew have been found, Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev told reporters, without specifying how many people were missing.
The attack "constitutes a flagrant violation of maritime law and, more broadly, of the rules of navigation", Radev said.
"Such an attack within Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone is absolutely unacceptable," he told reporters.
"Two merchant vessels were attacked by sea and air drones. This has been formally confirmed by the crews, and both ships were hit," Radev added.
European Union chief Ursula von der Leyen said Tuesday that attacks on civilian shipping in the Black Sea were "unacceptable".
"While exact circumstances of these incidents are still being established, the developments are very concerning," von der Leyen wrote online.
A Bulgarian ferry, the Dioskuria, which was in the area, witnessed the explosion of the first ship and proceeded to the scene, joined by a Bulgarian Navy fast boat, which rescued two crew, one suffering from burns and the other from a head injury.
The other 16 crew members were rescued by border guard patrol boats.
Eleven of the rescued crew are Turkish and seven are Indian, according to Radev.
'Extremely difficult'
According to the available information, one vessel was carrying wheat and heading south, while the other – which sank – was sailing north, Radev said. Its cargo is unknown.
"The situation significantly complicates navigation in the Black Sea, drives up insurance premiums, and makes maritime traffic extremely difficult," Radev said.
"As I have long maintained, if this war is not halted in time, it will continue to expand its geographical reach and increase risks, including the risk of a global conflict," Radev added.

The government said it would convene an emergency meeting on Tuesday to discuss the strikes.

articles.title: October 7, 3 years on: Can Gaza ceasefire pave the way for lasting Middle East peace? - Khaleej Times
articles.summary: October 7, 3 years on: Can Gaza ceasefire pave the way for lasting Middle East peace?  Khaleej Times
articles.full_text:
Three years ago, the Middle East entered a conflict that would extend far beyond Gaza. On October 7, 2023, Hamas-led fighters attacked southern Israel, killing around 1,200 people and taking 251 hostages into Gaza.
Israel responded with a military campaign that has killed tens of thousands of Palestinians, displaced most of the territory's population and left widespread destruction.
Three years later, large-scale hostilities in Gaza have stopped under a ceasefire that took effect on October 10, 2025. All remaining Israeli hostages and their remains have since been returned, according to UN.
But the violence has not completely stopped. Israeli strikes and military operations have continued, Palestinian casualties are still being reported and major political questions over Gaza's future remain unresolved.
The conflict also transformed the wider region, with fighting and tensions involving Lebanon, Iran and Yemen at different points over the past three years.
Today, the question is no longer only how the conflict began, but whether the region can prevent another cycle of violence.
Has the Gaza ceasefire brought peace?
Not yet. The October 2025 ceasefire brought an end to large-scale fighting and enabled the return of the remaining hostages, making it one of the most significant steps towards de-escalation since the war began.
But a ceasefire is not the same as peace. The UN said in its September 2026 report that Israeli airstrikes, shelling, drone attacks and ground operations have continued in Gaza, while Hamas and other armed groups have not disarmed.
Around two-thirds of Gaza also remains inaccessible or under severe access restrictions, according to the report.
Nearly a year after the ceasefire was announced, Palestinian casualties are also continuing.
According to figures from Gaza's Ministry of Health cited by the UN, 1,431 Palestinians had been reported killed between the ceasefire announcement and September 30, 2026.
This leaves the ceasefire in a difficult position: it has prevented a return to the scale of fighting seen during the war, but it has not ended violence.
What has changed across the region?
The consequences of the war did not remain within Gaza. Over the past three years, the Middle East has experienced periods of direct confrontation and heightened tensions involving Israel, Lebanon, Iran and Yemen.
That has made preventing escalation on one front increasingly connected to stability on others.
In June, UN Secretary-General António Guterres called on parties to fully respect ceasefires in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran and warned against actions that could undermine diplomatic efforts.
He said there was no military solution to the region's conflicts and called for dialogue and negotiations instead. The danger is that an incident on one front can quickly increase tensions elsewhere.
In July, amid renewed confrontations in the Gulf, the UN warned that a return to full-scale hostilities would have serious consequences not only for people in the region, but also for international security and the global economy.
Why does Gaza remain central to regional stability?
Even with large-scale fighting reduced, conditions inside Gaza remain severe. The UN says widespread destruction, continued strikes, restrictions on essential supplies and funding shortages are preventing recovery from moving at the scale required.
In late September, 94 per cent of Gaza's population was assessed as being in urgent need of shelter and basic household assistance, while 65 per cent of households were living in tents or makeshift shelters.
Thousands of damaged buildings also remain dangerous. More than 4,000 unsafe buildings require full or partial demolition, according to preliminary estimates cited by the UN, while more than 2,300 of them remain inhabited by nearly 44,000 people.
Without reconstruction and improved living conditions, humanitarian agencies warn that the effects of the war will continue long after major fighting has stopped.
The UN has also stressed that recovery cannot be separated from politics. Its September report said sustainable stability requires progress in Gaza alongside strengthening Palestinian institutions and establishing a credible political path towards resolving the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.
What could trigger another escalation?
The ceasefires across the region remain fragile. Continued strikes in Gaza, unresolved questions over security and governance, tensions involving armed groups and disputes over the implementation of ceasefire agreements all create risks.
The situation in the West Bank adds another source of pressure. The UN has reported high levels of settler violence, displacement and settlement expansion, warning in September that these developments were damaging prospects for peace.
Tensions elsewhere can also quickly affect the wider region. That is why the UN has repeatedly urged parties to avoid retaliatory actions, respect existing ceasefires and use diplomatic channels before incidents develop into broader confrontations.
What is needed to prevent another cycle of violence?
The first challenge is keeping existing ceasefires in place. That means preventing attacks and retaliatory actions from gradually weakening agreements until large-scale fighting returns.
The second is protecting civilians and improving humanitarian access. Despite the Gaza ceasefire, the UN says humanitarian access remains restricted and essential medical, shelter and infrastructure needs remain severe.
Reconstruction is another major challenge. Homes, hospitals, roads, water systems and other infrastructure will require years of rebuilding. Without visible improvements in daily life, the humanitarian crisis risks becoming a long-term source of instability.
But de-escalation also requires diplomacy beyond Gaza. The UN has called for ceasefires in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran to be respected and for regional disputes to be addressed through negotiations rather than military action.
Finally, there is the unresolved Israeli-Palestinian conflict itself. A ceasefire can stop or reduce fighting, but without a political process addressing the underlying conflict, the risk of renewed violence remains.
Three years after October 7, the region is no longer where it was in the weeks and months that followed the attack. Large-scale fighting in Gaza has stopped, hostages have returned and diplomatic efforts have produced periods of de-escalation. Civilians continue to die, Gaza remains devastated and tensions across the region remain fragile.
The challenge now is turning ceasefires into something more permanent. After three years of conflict, preventing the next escalation may depend not only on stopping violence when it begins, but on addressing the conditions that allow it to return.

articles.title: Trump: US must 'finish up' war with Iran the 'nice way or the not-so-nice way' - Gulf News
articles.summary: Trump: US must 'finish up' war with Iran the 'nice way or the not-so-nice way'  Gulf News
articles.full_text:
US pushes Iran for nuclear concessions amid escalating Middle East tensions
US President Donald Trump stated that the US must "finish up" the war with Iran, adding that Washington will soon decide whether to bring the conflict to an end the "nice way or the not-so-nice way."
During an address at an Anduril Industries event in Sparrows Point, Maryland, on October 6, 2026, Trump told attendees that the US was doing "extremely well" against Iran.
He declared that its military capabilities had been effectively neutralised: "They have no military in sight. The whole place is shot. They were the bully of the Middle East, and they're not so much the bully anymore."
By giving a choice between the "nice way or the not-so-nice way," Trump implied an upcoming choice between a diplomatic settlement or an intensified military campaign aimed at forced resolution.
Also In This Package
Trump reiterated that Tehran will not be allowed to obtain a nuclear weapon and addressed domestic concerns over rising energy costs, calling higher gas prices a "small price to pay for keeping the world safe" while promising prices would fall sharply once the war concludes.
Trump and Anduril unveiled plans Tuesday for a new “software-defined” shipyard that will help build attack submarines for the Navy faster.
The announcement comes as the Navy aims to boost its undersea arsenal, which could play a key role in a potential future conflict, even as Trump seeks to enhance domestic manufacturing.
Trump also stated in a press exchange on October 6, 2026, that his "biggest problem" in dealing with the conflict with Tehran is that "nobody knows who the hell is running" Iran after successive tiers of Iranian leadership were eliminated.
Speaking to reporters before boarding Marine One at the White House, Trump remarked: "Their leaders are gone, their second group of leaders are gone, and the biggest problem I have is nobody knows who the hell is running the country."
The comments come eight months into the active US-Israeli conflict with Iran that began in late February 2026.
Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei was killed at the onset of the conflict, and his designated successor, Mojtaba Khamenei, was severely injured in the same strike and has not been seen in public since. Subsequent leadership structures and high-ranking military commanders have also been targeted.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei pushed back on Trump's statements during a press conference.
Baghaei asserted that Washington knows full well how Iran's decision-making structure works.
Baghaei pushed the fault back onto Washington, citing "contradictory positions and mixed messaging from US officials".
Trump's shifting statements on timeline and objectives come as energy prices surge across global markets, adding domestic political pressure ahead of the upcoming US midterm elections.
Meanwhile, US Vice President JD Vance stated in an interview with journalists late on Tuesday (Oct. 6, 2026), that Iran must make a "meaningful" and "significant" reduction in its nuclear enrichment capacity to satisfy Washington's demands and bring an end to the ongoing conflict.
Vance emphasised that Washington remains open to a diplomatic agreement, but Iran must demonstrate concrete nuclear concessions — specifically scaling back its uranium enrichment infrastructure — to secure a permanent ceasefire.
The demand for enrichment reductions comes after earlier claims by administration officials that Iran's nuclear capabilities had been largely dismantled in initial strikes, highlighting ongoing concerns over underground infrastructure and surviving stockpiles.
Both nations have exchanged diplomatic proposals in recent weeks targeting an end to hostilities and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, a critical bottleneck for global energy shipping. However, President Donald Trump recently rejected Tehran's latest proposal as insufficient.
After 220 days of war, disruptions in energy markets and rising gas prices have added intense domestic pressure on the administration as the US midterm elections approach.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian previously characterized peace talks as "meaningless" while US-Israeli strikes continue, though foreign ministry officials have maintained that Washington is well aware of Iran's negotiating channels.

articles.title: Lithuania takes further step towards lifting nuclear weapons ban - Euronews.com
articles.summary: Lithuania takes further step towards lifting nuclear weapons ban  Euronews.com
articles.full_text:
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said on Tuesday that Lithuania’s move, alongside broader plans to expand US and NATO military infrastructure in the region, risked further escalating tensions.
Lithuania has taken a step towards removing a constitutional ban on nuclear weapons from its territory, bringing the Baltic state closer to the legal position of its neighbours as European allies debate how to strengthen NATO’s deterrence in the face of Russia.
The Lithuanian parliament, the Seimas, voted 106-18, with six abstentions, on Tuesday to advance a constitutional amendment removing a provision that bars weapons of mass destruction and foreign military bases from Lithuanian territory.
The change still requires a second vote after a constitutionally mandated three-month waiting period. At least 94 of the Seimas’ 141 members must back it on both occasions. The final vote is expected on January 12.
“This constitutional amendment would enable Lithuania’s armed forces to participate fully in the planning and exercises of all of NATO’s deterrence measures,” said Viktorija Čmilytė-Nielsen, leader of the Liberal Movement parliamentary group.
Currently, Article 137 of the Lithuanian Constitution stipulates that weapons of mass destruction and military bases of foreign states may not be located in Lithuania, which borders Belarus and Russia’s Kaliningrad exclave. This means that under current laws, allied aircraft or ships carrying nuclear weapons could not enter Lithuanian territory for deterrence purposes.
Added urgency in Lithuania's case
Supporters of the amendment argue that the constitutional provision has become a legal obstacle to Lithuania’s full participation in NATO’s nuclear deterrence arrangements and leaves the country at a disadvantage compared with other NATO allies.
“Our neighbouring countries, such as Latvia, Estonia and Poland, have no such restrictions either,” Remigijus Motuzas, chairman of the Seimas Foreign Affairs Committee, said during a parliamentary session in September. “We cannot be less protected than other NATO countries. We must send a signal that Lithuania is a full part of NATO’s nuclear deterrence.”
NATO describes nuclear deterrence as part of its collective defence, alongside conventional and missile-defence capabilities. The Alliance also says its nuclear policy remains consistent with its commitments to arms control, disarmament and non-proliferation.
For Lithuania, the issue has taken on added urgency. “NATO deterrence, including nuclear deterrence, is part of collective defence,” Motuzas said, adding that Russia has rapidly modernised its nuclear arsenal in recent years and deployed nuclear weapons close to Lithuania — in Kaliningrad and Belarus.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said on Tuesday that Lithuania’s move, alongside broader plans to expand US and NATO military infrastructure in the region, risked further escalating tensions, Reuters reported.
The warnings come as Russia has stepped up its nuclear rhetoric towards NATO. Moscow recently threatened nuclear retaliation in the event of what it described as attempts to isolate its Kaliningrad exclave, which borders Lithuania and Poland.
Finland has already made the move
Lithuania is not acting in isolation.
Finland, which joined NATO in 2023 after decades of military non-alignment, removed its own statutory prohibition on nuclear weapons earlier this year, citing the need to ensure that Finnish law did not restrict the country’s ability to fulfil its obligations as a NATO ally.
In June, the Finnish parliament approved amendments to the Nuclear Energy Act repealing the country’s ban on nuclear explosives. The legislation entered into force on July 1.
“This historic reform strengthens the security of Finland and of NATO as a whole,” Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen said on X.
Helsinki has stressed, however, that the change does not mean Finland intends to acquire or host nuclear weapons, and that NATO has no plans to station them there.
Finland has since joined a French-led initiative aimed at strengthening European security through closer cooperation on nuclear deterrence. French President Emmanuel Macron has proposed what Paris calls “forward deterrence” — closer cooperation with European allies around France’s independent nuclear capabilities.
The United Kingdom, Germany, Poland, Sweden, the Netherlands, Belgium, Greece, Denmark, and Norway have already signed up to France's initiative.

articles.title: As Trump Dithers, Ukraine War Is Approaching a ‘Fatal Point of No Return’ - Yahoo
articles.summary: As Trump Dithers, Ukraine War Is Approaching a ‘Fatal Point of No Return’  YahooSee more headlines & perspectives on Google News
articles.full_text:
The war in Ukraine is becoming increasingly dangerous, with the risk of escalation spilling further into Europe. As Russia and European governments trade explicit warnings that the conflict is spreading, the United States is pursuing diplomacy aimed less at stopping the carnage than restoring ties with Moscow.
With the Russian military making little progress on the ground in eastern Ukraine despite nearly five years of war and more than a million casualties, the Kremlin is intensifying aerial attacks. Ukraine, which has been the target of Russian missiles and drones since the war began in February 2022, is now experiencing a sharp uptick in attacks on infrastructure and populated areas that threaten to plunge parts of the country into cold and darkness over the winter.
The aerial blitzkrieg is intended to destroy Ukraine's morale, infrastructure, and economy, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy recently told the Financial Times, citing intelligence intercepted by his country's security services.
Zelenskyy told the paper that Russian President Vladimir Putin, in discussions with top Kremlin officials, had removed constraints on the bombardment campaign: "He said there are no rules now."
U.S. disengagement from the conflict during Trump's second term, coupled with the American president's animosity toward Zelenskyy and Ukraine more generally, has only emboldened Putin. After promising he would stop the war "within 24 hours" after reelection, Trump's tepid support for Ukraine and its European allies has increasingly convinced the Kremlin it has a chance to permanently rupture the NATO alliance.
At the Valdai Discussion Club on Thursday — an annual high-profile international summit in St. Petersburg — Putin said that continued European support for Ukraine was pushing the conflict toward a "fatal point of no return."
The Kremlin has long described the war as an extension of a confrontation with the collective West. With more than 1.5 million active service members in the Russian military, about 44 percent of Moscow's budget for 2027 is dedicated to defense and security spending. Around 700,000 Russian soldiers are serving on the front lines in Ukraine, where casualties remain staggeringly high.
Meanwhile, Moscow is conducting a campaign of so-called "hybrid warfare" — with officials in multiple countries alleging that a series of drone attacks, arsons, and sabotage originated with Russian intelligence services. The Kremlin also continues to carry out targeted killings on European soil — and has even attempted to assassinate political dissidents in the United States, according to the FBI.
Russia's belligerent activity has set alarm bells ringing across Europe.
Speaking at a NATO event on Thursday, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said that the continent must brace for "severe hybrid attacks," as Russia targets production facilities and logistics hubs by which Ukraine's allies supply the beleaguered country with arms. Europe must be prepared to "respond quickly and very clearly" to Russian provocations, Merz said.
For its part, Moscow asserts that NATO is provoking conflict, citing recent unannounced military exercises near Kaliningrad — a Russian exclave on the Baltic coast. In a communiqué to NATO this week, Russian officials warned that action against Kaliningrad would initiate a serious response, "including nuclear weapons" in order to defend its territory, and "Russian strikes against decision-making centers in the alliance's member states."
"This is a war that Europe is waging against us," Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov told reporters at the Valdai forum. When asked about hybrid attacks outside Ukraine that European leaders have attributed to Russia, he said his country was only targeting support for what it dubs the "Nazi regime" in Kyiv.
As the sabers rattle louder, American engagement with Moscow and Kyiv comes in fits and starts, with no apparent overarching strategy.
Critics of the White House's approach point to a recent trip by Trump's friend and special envoy to the Middle East, real estate attorney Steve Witkoff, and son-in-law Jared Kushner, to Moscow and Kyiv. Their tour yielded headlines, but little progress toward negotiations between the warring parties — let alone toward ending the conflict.
"I hope they had a great discussion about opening a hotel or something," one European official told Rolling Stone. "Because it was useless otherwise."
Diplomacy via haphazard tête-à-têtes with the president's personal envoys is almost certainly viewed as a sign of weakness by Putin, who is well aware that Trump hopes to claim normalized ties between the United States and Russia as a crowning foreign policy achievement.
The White House is considering a range of unprecedented diplomatic deals that would help keep Russia's economy functioning while doing little to benefit Ukraine.
These proposals reportedly include an easing of economic sanctions if Putin agrees to release some political prisoners, and a potential multibillion-dollar oil deal ostensibly aimed at stabilizing energy markets and reducing gas prices.
With gas prices rising amid the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran and midterm elections around the corner, Trump has made energy central to his Russia policy. Washington has called for an "energy ceasefire" — while Trump has blamed Kyiv for rising diesel prices in the United States.
While high oil prices are the result of a concatenation of crises, Ukraine has been targeting Russian oil refineries, producing fuel shortages and long queues for gasoline — in one of the world's largest oil producers — over the summer.
Ukraine is also developing its own domestically produced tactical ballistic missiles. Ukrainian officials said Friday that one type of missile, the FP-7, had been successfully used in combat for the first time. But whether Kyiv can produce enough of them to create a meaningful deterrent is unclear.
As winter nears, the outlook for Ukraine is bleak. A recent attack on Kyiv consisted of nearly a dozen ballistic missiles and hundreds of drones in a single night. That many munitions slip through highlights the dire situation faced by Ukrainian defenders, who are running out of advanced missile interceptors. They also struggle to shoot down drones that are becoming increasingly numerous, sophisticated, and effective as the war drags on.
In recent months, Russia has adopted widespread use of an advanced drone, the Geran-5 — a jet-powered drone that bears an uncanny resemblance to the V-1 "buzz bombs" used by the Nazis to bombard London toward the end of World War II.
As with the German V-1 campaign against London 80 years ago, the targets are often indiscriminate. Even before the ramping-up of attacks this fall, 2026 was on track to be the deadliest year for Ukrainian civilians since the early months of the full-scale war in 2022.
The proliferation of Russian attack drones and ballistic missiles means that cities like Kyiv now spend much of each day under air alert. Even aside from the human toll and physical damage that the weapons inflict, officials estimate that the disruptions to daily life are costing the country as much as $45 million per hour in lost economic activity.
Since Friday, a series of drone attacks has targeted two of Kyiv's major bridges spanning the Dnieper River. The damage has disrupted traffic between the capital's "Right Bank" — with its historic core and city center — and its "Left Bank," with its sprawling Soviet-era industrial and residential developments.
Ukraine is already experiencing a severe financial squeeze. Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi says the country is facing a $27 billion "funding gap" before the end of the year.
Ukrainian lawmakers warn the government could even run out of funds to pay soldiers. One serving member of the Ukrainian military, who spoke to Rolling Stone on background, said by the end of the summer, members of his unit had already begun experiencing "delays" in receiving their pay.
The Ministry of Defense disputes that soldier's salaries could go unpaid, but acknowledges that "technical issues" had caused some delays.
Meanwhile, Zelenskyy is under pressure from corruption scandals and resignations involving members of his inner circle. Polls show him potentially losing hypothetical match-ups against rivals, including former Ukrainian Armed Forces commander Valerii Zaluzhny. The country's "long-admired cohesion" has begun to crack — an outcome that aligns with Russia's strategic objectives.
But after nearly five years of war, both combatants are showing signs of political and economic strain.
Russia's regular military conscription process — 120,000 new recruits are expected over the next three months — barely offsets the grievous casualties its military is experiencing at the Ukrainian front, with high estimates exceeding 1,000 casualties per day.
Some analysts believe the Kremlin is considering a massive mobilization in the wake of parliamentary elections. But Putin so far has merely called for an increase in the total number of active-duty military members by a little more than 15,000. Russia's president remains wary of generating a meaningful anti-war movement inside Russia, while also facing pressure from hard-line nationalists expecting him to deliver victory.

articles.title: Russia testing Europe's defenses below threshold of open war, experts say - The Kyiv Independent
articles.summary: Russia testing Europe's defenses below threshold of open war, experts say  The Kyiv Independent
articles.full_text:
Russia is testing how far it can push Europe without triggering open war — from drones crossing NATO airspace to sabotage and cyberattacks across the continent. Experts warn that Europe has strengthened its defenses since 2022, but key gaps remain, including in air defense, communications, intelligence, and joint command.
Russia is testing the limits of Europe's security without formally crossing into open war. Its attacks on Ukrainian cities have intensified in recent months, including strikes on civilian infrastructure. Russian drones entering NATO airspace have also become a recurring occurrence, while Western officials have raised the alarm over a rise in Moscow's hybrid operations across Europe.
In September, Germany accused Russia of orchestrating an attempted drone attack at Leipzig Airport in early August. The incidents are raising a broader question: how far Moscow can escalate its pressure on European countries without prompting a direct military response.
The Kyiv Independent spoke with participants of the Ukraine Recovery Lab, sponsored by Erste Foundation and organized as part of the European Forum Alpbach in Austria, held Aug. 24-Sept 4.
What may look like a string of hybrid incidents increasingly resembles a sub-threshold war against Europe, says Olena Davlikanova, a security policy expert.
The Everywhere War Tracker records a sustained campaign of sabotage, cyberattacks, military provocations, and airspace violations, which has grown more intensive and audacious since 2024 as Moscow has tested how far it can push Europe without triggering open conflict.
"Russia is waging a war against the European model of freedom, equality, and solidarity, and against the institutions that sustain it, especially the EU. This is a war fought in small steps," says Leopold Schmertzing, а strategic foresight and security and defense policy expert.
"I struggle to see it ending without a fundamental change in either the current Russian model or the European one."
Schmertzing argues that, despite Europe contributing far more to Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine than it did to earlier conflicts, most Europeans still experience it as a war happening somewhere else.
"My fear is that we will only fully wake up when our own capitals are attacked and our citizens are killed. By then, it will be too late to prepare," he added.
Experts believe Europe is better prepared for a potential confrontation with Russia than it was in 2022, but important gaps remain. Air defense, drones, communications, intelligence and joint command remain weak points, they say, while European militaries have yet to fully adapt to the realities of modern warfare.
Ukraine's experience shows that unmanned systems can have an outsized impact, but European defense spending has yet to reflect that lesson.
More than 80% of Russian targets destroyed on the battlefield are hit by drones, President Volodymyr Zelensky said in January.
"That is how the modern war looks like," says Kateryna Mykhalko, managing director of the German-Ukrainian defense industry consortium New Age Defense.
"At the same time, the technology delivering 80% of battlefield results receives only roughly 2% of European defense budgets," she adds.
The EU and Ukraine have sought to deepen cooperation in the sector. The EU-Ukraine Drone Alliance aims to accelerate the development and production of drones and counter-drone systems, combining Ukraine’s battlefield experience with Europe’s industrial capacity.
For Europe, the challenge is therefore twofold: closing military capability gaps while developing a response to forms of Russian aggression that experts believe are already unfolding across the continent.
"Russia is a hard nut to crack because it is deeply vulnerable in some respects and remarkably insulated in others," Schmertzing says. "We have a great deal to learn from Ukraine about where pressure works and where it doesn't."

articles.title: Centrii warns nation-state access and renewable supply-chain risks raise energy sector financial exposure - Industrial Cyber
articles.summary: Centrii warns nation-state access and renewable supply-chain risks raise energy sector financial exposure  Industrial Cyber
articles.full_text:
New analysis from Centrii identified that cyber risk in the energy sector is increasingly becoming a financial and geopolitical concern as nation-state activity, ransomware and renewable-energy supply-chain risks converge. In an Oct. 1 analysis, the company said state-linked actors are increasingly positioning themselves inside energy infrastructure for potential future disruption, while criminal ransomware attacks are creating measurable financial exposure for utilities.
“Over the past several months, nation-state activity, criminal ransomware, and a supply chain crisis have converged into something that looks less like a security problem and more like a portfolio risk,” Centrii detailed in its most recent analysis. “If you sit on a board, manage a fund, or run risk for a utility or an IPP, this is now your problem too, not just your CISO’s.”
Centrii pointed to Volt Typhoon’s reported footholds in U.S. critical infrastructure and an updated U.S. advisory on Iranian-affiliated actors exploiting internet-facing programmable logic controllers, alongside reported Russian-attributed sabotage activity in Europe. The analysis also highlighted growing cybersecurity concerns around renewable-energy supply chains, particularly grid-connected solar inverters and battery systems.
It noted that the most consequential shift in the threat landscape this year is not a specific breach, despite the serious nature of those attacks. But rather the change in intent, wherein security agencies and researchers now describe multiple state-linked actors as pre-positioning inside energy infrastructure rather than simply gathering intelligence.
“A China-linked group publicly known as Volt Typhoon has maintained footholds inside US critical infrastructure networks for years, using legitimate administrative tools rather than malware, making it much harder to detect,” the post observed. “US agencies have found no confirmed evidence that the group has been fully removed. The consistent assessment across investigators is that this activity is meant to enable disruption of US energy, water, and communications systems during a future crisis, not to steal data today.”
A recently updated joint advisory from U.S. federal agencies describes ongoing exploitation of internet-facing programmable logic controllers by Iranian-affiliated actors, with energy sector systems named specifically among the affected deployments.
In Europe, the activity has moved beyond cyber intrusion into physical sabotage. Reported incidents include a plot to disable undersea cables using submersible technology, and a drone sabotage attempt at a European airport involving military-grade explosives, both attributed to Russia by Western officials. Independent industry threat assessments have separately flagged that distributed renewable and grid-edge assets, the fastest-growing part of the generation mix, carry weaker security governance than traditional generation, and represent a growing share of the exposure.
None of this requires a successful attack to matter financially. Pre-positioned access inside a network is already a portfolio risk the moment an insurer, a lender, or an investment committee asks whether it can be ruled out.
Centrii also touched upon how renewable supply chains are now being treated as a national security issue. A large majority of solar inverters installed across Europe come from a small number of Chinese manufacturers, and inverters are the component that links solar and storage assets to the grid. Researchers have publicly disclosed flaws in widely deployed inverters that could let a nearby attacker shut units down, change their output, or push unauthorized firmware using only an intercepted serial number. Investigators have also reported undocumented cellular hardware in inverters and batteries from several Chinese suppliers, capable of bypassing the firewalls utilities use to block outside access.
Regulators on both sides of the Atlantic see this as a structural risk rather than a single-vendor problem. The European Commission has restricted EU funding for renewable projects that use inverters from a list of high-risk suppliers, warning that a coordinated remote shutdown could cause blackouts across several member states. In the US, a new executive order declares a national emergency over the bulk-power system and restricts transactions involving foreign-linked equipment, including grid-connected inverters, battery storage, and industrial control systems, even for equipment already under contract. For anyone acquiring renewable or storage assets, unknown inverter provenance is now a financial and regulatory exposure that needs to be priced into the deal.
“State-linked pre-positioning gets the headlines, but criminal ransomware is doing the most measurable financial damage right now,” Centrii reported. “Utility sector ransomware incidents rose sharply in the first quarter of 2026 compared with prior months, spread across more than a dozen countries. Broader industry analysis has found that energy, oil, and utilities organizations face ransomware at a materially higher rate than the average across other sectors, with most of those incidents resulting in encrypted operational data.”
Moreover, the financial pattern is consistent. Attackers know that recovery costs in the energy sector run well into the millions per incident, and organizations without tested recovery processes for OT environments specifically tend to take far longer to restore service than their IT-only counterparts. That’s leverage.
Regulation, especially for renewables, has lagged the threat landscape for years, but it is now catching up. NIS2, the EU’s cybersecurity directive, has moved from transposition into active enforcement, with member state authorities running audit programs aimed specifically at the energy sector and imposing real fines rather than warnings. The EU’s Critical Entities Resilience Directive, NIS2’s physical counterpart, required member states to formally designate critical entities by mid-2026, including electricity, storage, and demand response operators. Once designated, those entities have a defined window to meet the full set of requirements, which cover supply chain dependencies, incident handling, and continuity planning, not just cyber controls.
In the U.S., NERC CIP-015 is lowering the capacity threshold that triggers mandatory internal network monitoring. This pulls a much larger share of solar, wind, and storage assets into scope just as inverter-based resources become the fastest-growing part of the grid. TSA’s pipeline security directives extend a comparable monitoring and reporting obligation to midstream oil and gas operators. The executive order restricting foreign-linked grid equipment serves as a compliance answer to the supply chain problem, since it is intended to address what gets installed before it becomes a monitoring burden after the fact.
“Together, these frameworks are pushing the industry away from static, point-in-time compliance documents and toward continuous, timely evidence about monitoring, governance, and incident response,” according to Centrii. “At their core, these frameworks are effective security measures that protect lives and keep operators sustainable over the long run, not just compliance checkboxes. The evidence they require also lets companies prove that resilience continuously, rather than once a year at audit time.”
Centrii said that the insurance market will soon become one of the more effective enforcement mechanisms. Global cyber insurance premiums have risen sharply, and underwriters have shifted from questionnaire-based applications to technical audits of an applicant’s environment. For energy and utility operators specifically, that increasingly means demonstrable, dated evidence of OT monitoring controls, not a vendor attestation, before a policy renews at a reasonable rate.
“This closes the loop,” it added. “Regulators set the requirement, but enforcement was slow and inconsistent. Insurers now sit on the other side of the same requirement with a much faster feedback mechanism: your premium, your deductible, and in some cases whether you can get coverage at all.”
Taken together, the shape of the problem is clear. Nation-state actors are positioning for disruption, not just intelligence collection. The renewable supply chain behind the energy transition carries a vendor risk that did not exist in this form five years ago. And criminal ransomware crews have learned that utilities will pay when the leverage is right. Regulators, insurers, and investment committees- the three groups with the power to force a response- are now asking the same question at the same time: can an operator prove, continuously and with evidence, that it has visibility into its own operational environment and controls in place to protect it?
“Operators that can answer that question with real, current evidence are turning a compliance cost into a credential with lenders, insurers, and acquirers,” Centrii wrote in its analysis. “Operators that cannot will find out how expensive that gap is at the worst possible moment, whether that’s a renewal letter, an audit finding, or a disruption that reaches the board before the security team has finished writing the incident report.”

Batteries help keep the grid’s frequency stable, and that balancing is increasingly managed through cloud platforms controlling thousands of units at once. The report argues an attacker would not need to halt generation to cause a blackout, only to push batteries into synchronized charge and discharge patterns.

articles.full_text:
The world is facing a record-breaking El Nino this year, and weather experts say governments need to prepare now as 'death and severe illness' are on the cards
Weather experts are urging governments across the world to “act now” as El Nino is set to intensify significantly before the end of the year.
El Nino occurs every few years when temperatures in the tropical eastern Pacific rise 0.5C above the long-term average. For the UK, it tends to lead to wetter and stormier conditions in the winter months, and extreme heat during the summer.
Experts say the current El Nino is likely to be the strongest in living memory. Celeste Saulo, Secretary-General of the World Meteorological Organization (WMO), says “we still have time to act” and called on health authorities across the world to treat extreme heat “as the predictable public-health risk that it is”.
Much of the Southern Hemisphere will face its hottest months at the start of 2027, just as El Nino will be peaking. The WMO says “death and severe illness” are on the cards as the extreme conditions will exacerbate preexisting health conditions.
But the heat isn’t the only risk. Armel Castellan, Extreme Heat Advisor from the WHO-WMO Climate and Health Joint Programme, says: “WMO’s seasonal climate outlook for September to November points to above-normal rainfall in some regions and drought risk in others. That puts water security, nutrition, and vector-borne disease on the table alongside temperature.
“The WMO seasonal outlooks buy us much needed lead time, and that lead time is what lets health authorities look ahead and prepare, rather than repair. If health practitioners can make informed decisions, this can make the difference between losing lives or saving them.”
