Warmer temperatures and changing rainfall patterns also bring an increased risk of diseases carried by mosquitoes, the WMO says. Malaria, dengue, chikungunya, yellow fever and Zika could all spread to regions where they are not usually seen.
The WMO identified malnutrition and cholera as among the “most serious concerns” in regions facing both drought and flooding. Moreover, the amount of people facing acute food insecurity is expected to rise - and it already stands at 150 million globally.
Teresa Zakaria, Unit Head for Risk Reduction, Humanitarian Operations and Climate Change at WHO, said: “El Nino is a significant public health threat, not just a climate phenomenon. It is a risk multiplier, and we expect to see health impacts across the world.
“However, the most severe impacts will be experienced where climate shocks intersect with weak health systems, limited access to health care, food insecurity, displacement and humanitarian crises.”

articles.title: Andrew takes legal action over search warrants before his arrest - BBC
articles.summary: Andrew takes legal action over search warrants before his arrest  BBCAndrew Mountbatten-Windsor takes legal action against UK police over search warrants before arrest  CNNAndrew Mountbatten-Windsor takes police to court over Epstein files arrest  ReutersEx-Prince Andrew Can’t Use Money from Brother King Charles in Legal Action Against Police  People.comBuckingham Palace says it will not fund Andrew’s legal action against police  The Guardian
articles.full_text:
Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor is taking legal action against Thames Valley Police over search warrants issued before his arrest in February.
The former Prince Andrew was arrested on suspicion of misconduct in public office, in the wake of information that emerged from the Epstein files in the United States. Mountbatten-Windsor has consistently denied any wrongdoing linked to his association with Epstein.
His lawyers are understood to be challenging the lawfulness of search warrants used for Sandringham and at Royal Lodge in Windsor relating to his arrest, as first reported by the Telegraph.
A royal source has made clear that while the King provides a private allowance for Mountbatten-Windsor, this money is not to be used to fund such a judicial review.
Thames Valley Police confirmed it faced a legal challenge over the search warrants: "We are engaged in legal proceedings in relation to warrants previously obtained from the Central Criminal Court."
It added: "As these legal proceedings are currently ongoing, it would be inappropriate for us to comment further."
Mountbatten-Windsor, who lost his titles as a prince and Duke of York over his connections to the sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, wants a judicial review to consider the legality of the search warrants.
A court hearing will be held on Thursday afternoon as part of the process to consider this bid to quash the warrants, with the hearing set to begin in private. The judge will initially hear a request by the police to keep some documents private.
The warrants had been issued by a judge at the Central Criminal Court on 18 February - the day before Mountbatten-Windsor was arrested - and the legal challenge is an application for judicial review against the chief constable of Thames Valley Police and the Central Criminal Court.
"Even if Andrew succeeds in having the search warrants quashed, that would not necessarily be the victory it might first appear," said Nick Vamos, a criminal lawyer at Peters & Peters and former head of special crime at the Crown Prosecution Service.
Vamos said such disputes over warrants were not uncommon - but if the police lost on a technical error, they could still sometimes keep what they had obtained in a search.
"The police can apply back to the Crown Court to retain the material if they have grounds to immediately seize it again," said Vamos.
It would need to be a more fundamental issue with the granting of the warrants for the police to be required to return the material from a search, he said.
For several days after the arrest, police were seen searching Mountbatten-Windsor's property at Marsh Farm in Sandringham and at his former home, Royal Lodge, on the Windsor estate.
The arrest, carried out on his 66th birthday, followed a series of revelations from the Epstein files, published by the US Department of Justice.
They included emails appearing to show official documents being shared by Mountbatten-Windsor with Epstein and others, at a time when he was the UK's trade envoy.
Mountbatten-Windsor had already been stripped of his titles by King Charles, after emails had shown Mountbatten-Windsor had continued his links with Epstein, beyond when he had publicly said those links had been severed.
After Mountbatten-Windsor's arrest in February he was taken to Aylsham police station. A photograph captured his departure later that day, looking exhausted, after he was released under investigation.
The launch of this legal action against the police over the search warrants is the first public pushback from the former prince, who has lost his home, titles and public status, with charities and businesses distancing themselves from him.
Author Andrew Lownie said the legal move against Thames Valley could be a signal to the police to encourage them not to "pursue their investigations with such vigour in future".
But Mountbatten-Windsor's biographer called for other police forces to continue with their investigations - and that "diplomatic and international pressure needs to be put on the US Department of Justice to release the files".
Thames Valley Police says its investigation into Mountbatten-Windsor is continuing.
In a previous update it said the force had been "working with the United States Department of Justice to get further information that may be related to this investigation".
Detectives also highlighted that allegations of sexual misconduct could be considered as part of this inquiry into potential misconduct in public office.

articles.full_text:
Palestinians survey damage in a Rafah neighborhood in southern Gaza on Jan. 20, 2025, after returning following the start of a ceasefire between Israel and Hamas the previous day. Bashar Taleb/AFP/Getty Images
Joe Biden’s team and President-elect Donald Trump’s team coordinated their efforts to negotiate a ceasefire in Gaza and the release of hostages. Brett McGurk, who handled Middle East affairs and negotiations in the Biden administration, described the talks and a meeting between representatives of both teams on November 20, 2024, in his book “On the Brink: Behind the Scenes of the Fight to Free the October 7 Hostages.”
According to CNN
Efforts to reach an agreement stalled in August, when Hamas militants killed six hostages in a tunnel near Rafah. Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar and Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah were later killed, and Israel struck Iran. McGurk believed these events had shifted the balance of power and created an opportunity to return to negotiations.
How the Biden and Trump teams coordinated Gaza negotiations
After the election, McGurk suggested that Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law, coordinate the efforts of the two teams. He believed this would show Israel and Hamas that Biden and Trump’s representatives were acting together.
During a meeting at the Capitol, McGurk and National Security Advisor Jake Sullivan briefed their successors on the progress of the negotiations. Mike Waltz and Steve Witkoff attended on behalf of Trump’s incoming team. Vice President-elect JD Vance also joined the conversation briefly.
The only reason I’m here is to save lives. There’s nothing more noble than saving another person’s life. So I’m all in – you can count on me.
– Steve Witkoff
McGurk gave Witkoff a draft agreement. It covered the withdrawal of Israeli forces, an exchange of hostages and prisoners, and the delivery of humanitarian aid. One unresolved issue was which hostages Hamas would release in the first phase. According to McGurk, an agreement was impossible without settling that list.
Witkoff agreed to stay in regular contact and visit the region to restore lines of communication, but not to negotiate on his own. McGurk described the meeting as the beginning of cooperation between teams seeking to use the time before the transfer of power to advance an agreement on a ceasefire and the release of hostages.

- Israel confirms names of three deceased hostages returned; humanitarian aid to Gaza may be delayed amid ongoing negotiations.
- Israel received remains of one of the last fallen hostages from Hamas via the Red Cross, marking the fourth transfer this week amid ongoing hostage negotiations.
- CNN analyst Brett McGurk argues that Iran has not won the war and is gradually losing influence as shipping resumes through the Strait of Hormuz.

articles.title: The Myth of Military Victory
articles.summary: The dangerous idea driving today’s wars of choice.
articles.full_text:
Military victory is an alluring idea. A short, violent campaign that defeats the enemy promises payoffs at a tolerable price. The Trump administration expected such an outcome in Iran in February 2026. The Netanyahu government sought it in Gaza in October 2023, then in Lebanon and Iran. Russian President Vladimir Putin assumed his 2022 invasion of Ukraine would deliver it. Many critics of U.S. policy in Afghanistan and Iraq decry a failure to achieve military victory, contrasting such wars with the decisive battlefield outcomes they believe were achieved in the 1990–91 Gulf War and World War II. And until recently, the debate over U.S. aid to Ukraine featured widespread calls to help the country win a military victory, dismissing negotiations as appeasement.
Yet those who invoke the term rarely define it. “Victory” means achieving the political aims for which one went to war. But “military victory” implies more. The adjective signals that those aims are secured through combat rather than at the bargaining table. Negotiation requires compromise and invites stalling that can exhaust political will. Battlefield victory, by contrast, promises a prostrate enemy with no meaningful choice but to accept the victor’s terms on the victor’s timetable. That promise is what makes the idea so attractive and so ubiquitous.
But the notion of military victory is a dangerous myth. All modern wars end in negotiated settlements; talks are not a second-best fallback. To end a war, both sides must choose to stop fighting, and those choices always require nontrivial bargaining. Destruction matters, of course. It is what distinguishes war from peacetime politics. But its role is to shape the bargain, not to annihilate the enemy, which almost never happens.
The myth of military victory has repeatedly led governments to start or prolong wars on false premises about how those wars would end. The Trump administration believed force could compel Iran’s unconditional surrender; instead, the United States finds itself in a stalemate. The Netanyahu government’s conviction that it can defeat Hamas militarily has lengthened the Gaza war in pursuit of an unattainable goal. Putin’s expectation of battlefield victory in Ukraine has mired both countries in a war with no apparent endgame.
If Chinese leader Xi Jinping makes the same mistake, an attack on Taiwan could ensnare Beijing in a conflict that is easier to start than to stop, with stakes far beyond the Taiwan Strait. And if the United States assumes that it could secure a military victory in a war with China, then it, too, could find itself exhausted in a fight it cannot easily end.
Muddled thinking about how wars conclude also breeds prewar errors in intelligence, modernization, and force design. And misunderstanding the relationship between bargaining and fighting produces a systematic failure to integrate negotiating strategy with campaign planning. As long as policymakers do not grasp that wars end only when both sides are ready to lay down their arms, they will continue to be frustrated by the inability of military force to achieve their political goals.
CARTHAGE WAS THE EXCEPTION
No modern war has destroyed an enemy’s ability to resist. Combatants can always keep fighting if they choose, even after enemies sweep their military from the field or capture their capital. Such persistence can reverse fortunes and decide wars. Winning a war requires offering surviving (and potential) fighters a deal they prefer to continued resistance. These deals can be one-sided. But terms and bargaining always matter: no war ends unless both sides choose to accept a settlement and stop.
The only alternative is to physically annihilate one’s enemies. Rome succeeded in doing so when it ended the Third Punic War by enslaving Carthage’s surviving citizens and, according to legend, salting the city’s ruins so nothing would grow there again. But no war in the modern era has met this criterion, and few have come close. Since the Napoleonic Wars ended, in 1815, the defeated parties in interstate wars have lost a median of eight percent of their forces. In two-thirds of those cases, that figure was under ten percent. The only country to lose more than 90 percent of its forces was Paraguay, in the Triple Alliance War (1864–70). Most belligerents accept defeat—settlement on unfavorable terms—long before their capacity to resist runs out.
War-ending settlements can be explicit or tacit. Explicit negotiations involve direct communication, offers, and counteroffers; examples include the Korean War armistice and the 1995 Dayton accords that concluded the Bosnian war. Tacit bargaining uses actions, threats, or declarations to signal acceptance or rejection of terms without formal talks.
The 1990–91 Gulf War, for example, ended when the U.S.-led coalition announced a unilateral cease-fire, and the Iraqis stopped fighting, too, without diplomatic exchanges. Combat had shown Iraqi President Saddam Hussein that continued resistance would bring further coalition advances, potentially to Baghdad; the cease-fire signaled that U.S. and allied forces would hold their positions if the Iraqis did the same. Saddam understood and reciprocated. General Norman Schwarzkopf, the coalition commander, then instructed Baghdad to send a military delegation to Safwan airfield to negotiate disengagement. The result heavily favored the United States and its allies. They liberated Kuwait, their central aim. Saddam preserved his regime but lost his conquests and faced postwar restrictions, leaving him worse off than he was before his invasion.
 All modern wars end in negotiated settlements.
This was an unambiguous victory, but it was not achieved by destroying Iraq’s capacity to resist. At the cease-fire, the Iraqi army retained most of its prewar strength. Up to 50,000 Iraqi soldiers had been killed and 75,000 wounded out of a force exceeding a million—under 15 percent. Over 800,000 troops survived and could have kept fighting. Days later, Iraqi forces crushed Shiite uprisings in the south.
Saddam’s decision to stop in 1991 was not a mere acceptance of reality. Iraq’s experience in its next war with the United States shows why. In 2003, the Iraqi military disintegrated after just seven weeks of fighting, its soldiers abandoning posts, weapons, and commanders and shedding their uniforms. By mid-May, Saddam could bring far less military power to bear than at Safwan in 1991. If a country could ever end a war by disarming the enemy, the United States should have done so in Iraq by May 2003. It did not.
The Iraqi military could no longer hold ground or resist coalition advances, but many of its soldiers carried on, even after Baghdad fell and their only option was to resort to irregular tactics. Sunni Baathists understood the implicit terms on offer: life under a U.S.-installed Shiite government. They preferred to fight on. The U.S. military suffered fewer than 3,000 casualties in 2003 but more than 33,000 in the next eight years. The insurgents failed to restore Saddam’s regime, but the war did not end in 2003, when Baghdad fell and its uniformed military evaporated.
Afghanistan offers a similar example. By mid-2002, the U.S. invasion had disarmed the Taliban’s military, occupied Kabul, and driven the group’s leaders from the country. Like Iraqi Baathists a year later, the Taliban faced a dominant enemy controlling their homeland, with no immediate prospect of retaking the capital. If “military victory” can terminate a war, then Afghanistan, too, should have been a decisive U.S. success. It was not. Taliban survivors rejected the terms on offer—an Afghan government that excluded them—even though their situation was far bleaker than Saddam’s in 1991. They kept fighting as irregulars, and by 2021 they had recaptured Kabul, driven out U.S. forces, and restored their rule.
The elusiveness of military victory does not make battlefield effectiveness irrelevant. But the purpose of fighting is to shape the two sides’ bargaining leverage by shifting their expectations of future costs, not to annihilate the enemy. Success in combat enables productive talks, but it is no substitute for them.
TERMS OF SURRENDER
Perhaps the most frequently cited example of military victory—the imposition of a brute-force triumph on a prostrate enemy—is the Allied conquest of Nazi Germany and imperial Japan in World War II. In conflicts from Afghanistan to Ukraine to Gaza, policymakers and pundits invoke Germany’s and Japan’s ostensible military destruction in direct contrast to wars that ended with negotiated outcomes. Yet World War II did not end because the vanquished had no choice but surrender. The fighting did not disarm Germany or Japan. Both retained the capacity to inflict enormous casualties on the Allies, and neither surrendered unconditionally. The victors offered explicit terms—conditions—to both. These concessions were small, and the Allies unambiguously won. But even World War II ended in bargains between actors with options.
Imperial Japan fielded nearly eight million troops during the war. Fewer than two million died in combat. When Japan surrendered, in August 1945, more than six million armed, equipped, uniformed, and commanded soldiers remained in the field. These forces could not reclaim Japan’s conquests, which the Allies had steadily reversed since mid-1942. By the summer of 1945, the United States had driven the Japanese navy into port and severed Tokyo’s control of airspace and sea-lanes, leaving the Allies poised to invade Japan and depose Emperor Hirohito.
Yet Japan continued to resist—not because it expected to destroy the Allied militaries, or reconquer lost territory, or throw an invasion force into the sea, but because it sought to secure more tolerable settlement terms by threatening to kill more servicemen than the Allies were willing to sacrifice. articles.summary: Germany's former foreign intelligence chief arrested on suspicion of espionage and attempted treason  AP NewsFormer German spy chief arrested for attempted treason, obtaining state secrets  ReutersGermany’s beleaguered spies face a fresh scandal  Financial TimesGerman Officials Arrest Former Spy Chief on Espionage Charges  The New York TimesGermany arrests former intelligence chief over alleged spying  The Guardian

BERLIN (AP) — A former head of Germany ‘s foreign intelligence service was arrested Tuesday on suspicion that he had passed state secrets to a foreign intelligence service, the federal prosecutor’s office said.
August Hanning, who led the Federal Intelligence Service, known by its German acronym BND, from 1998 to 2005, is “strongly suspected of treasonous espionage, spying out state secrets, attempted treason, and espionage,” the federal prosecutor’s office said in a statement.
Hanning, 80, was arrested in Bad Toelz-Wolfratshausen in southern Germany. A former aide, identified as Manfred D., was also arrested Tuesday in Steinfurt in western Germany and has been charged with aiding and abetting attempted treason and treasonous espionage.
“In one instance, there is suspicion that Mr. Hanning used classified information to prepare an analysis for an employee of a foreign intelligence service,” Ines Peterson, a spokesperson for the federal prosecutor’s office, told German broadcaster RTL.
“In another instance, he is alleged to have passed on information following an extensive exchange — also with an employee of another intelligence service.”
Neither Peterson nor the earlier statement by the prosecutor’s office revealed who exactly the two men were suspected of spying for or which foreign intelligence services they provided with classified information.
Premises belonging to both men were searched Tuesday.
Former aide allegedly supplied Hanning with BND documents
The prosecutor’s office said Manfred D. worked as Hanning’s chief of staff and later served as chief of staff for several subsequent BND presidents from 2012 until 2026.
“In his role, he had access to confidential information,” the prosecutor’s office said.
Both suspects are believed to have agreed in 2010 to have Manfred D. continuously transmit valuable intelligence from the BND to Hanning in exchange for payment, the statement said.
“The current findings suggest that, over the years, Manfred D. provided Hanning with approximately 2,000 documents, many of which contained classified information to be used exclusively by the federal intelligence service for internal purposes, particularly for executive intelligence briefings,” the statement said.
Hanning used the information in private consulting work and Manfred D., who in line with German privacy rules cannot be identified by his full name, provided Hanning with classified information until June 2022, Peterson said.
Hanning is suspected of involvement in a prominent child abduction case
Hanning came under scrutiny in a separate investigation into the abduction of Hamburg businesswoman Christina Block’s children from her ex-husband in Denmark in January 2024 in a lengthy custody battle.
The investigation into that case led to Tuesday’s arrests.
The current proceedings stem from evidence found during a search of Hanning’s residence in connection with that case, the federal prosecutor’s office stated.
Hanning and a retired official from the Hamburg State Criminal Police Office are suspected of having accepted a contract from Block in 2022 to abduct her children while serving as executives of a security firm, the public prosecutor’s office announced in the fall of 2025, according to German news agency dpa.
The Blocks are a prominent Hamburg family best known for their popular national steakhouse chain Block House. The custody trial has received a lot of attention in the country, with German tabloids offering heavy coverage from the court.
A message to the BND for comment was not immediately returned.
German opposition lawmaker calls for a quick probe
German opposition lawmaker Konstantin von Notz expressed shock about the allegations against Hanning and called for a quick investigation.
“This is a hard-hitting and deeply troubling story,” said von Notz, a member of the Greens party and also the German parliament committee overseeing the intelligence services.
“We expect a swift and thorough investigation into the egregious allegations leveled against former BND chief Hanning,” he told Spiegel Online.
“We have been criticizing the dubious and wide-ranging lobbying activities of former top officials and those with the highest security clearances in Germany for years,” he said and called for banning former officials with security clearances from engaging in private consulting work after leaving office, Spiegel Online reported.

A top Democratic lawmaker is seeking information on Jared Kushner’s financial investments following a CNN investigation last week that found his private equity firm is the largest shareholder in an Israeli company backing businesses involved in Israel’s military campaigns.
Rep. Robert Garcia, the ranking member on the House Oversight Committee, sent Kushner’s investment firm, Affinity Partners, a letter on Monday saying Democrats on the committee were “investigating the unprecedented and dangerous ways in which President Trump and his family have profited directly from their access to power.
“…I request detailed information about your business dealings in the Middle East to understand whether your significant financial gains have come at the cost of Americans’ safety and security, ” the California representative wrote.
The letter is yet another sign that House Democrats are poised to investigate President Donald Trump’s family members’ business dealings overseas and in the US, should they retake the majority in the midterm elections this fall.
An attorney for Kushner dismissed Garcia’s criticisms and sought to draw attention to the congressman’s own holdings in investments scrutinized in CNN’s report on Kushner – Phoenix Financial, an Israeli financial services firm which counts Affinity Partners as its biggest investor, and Elbit Systems, Israel’s largest arms manufacturer.
“Rep. Garcia’s letter is a masterclass in irony: A member of Congress questioning a private citizen for having an interest in the same stock in which the member also holds an interest,” the attorney said in a statement to CNN. “Jared has no role in deciding what Phoenix buys or sells. But if that doesn’t matter to Rep. Garcia, he should begin by investigating himself.”
Garcia’s most recent disclosure forms indicate his pension plans are managed through the California Public Employees’ Retirement System and California State Teachers Retirement System. Both plans hold stock in Phoenix Financials or Elbit Systems.
A spokesperson for Garcia said Kushner’s attorney was trying to “deflect” from his client’s own conduct, adding the congressman does not trade stocks and, like the millions of other public employees in the pension plan, does not have any control over the fund and cannot opt out.
Kushner “makes millions with no accountability all while he travels the Middle East on behalf of his father in law,” said Sara Guerrero, Garcia’s spokesperson.
“The apparent conflict of interest between Affinity Partners’ investments and your work in the Middle East, and in particular the potential for corrupt dealmaking given those competing interests, demands congressional oversight and accountability,” Garcia’s letter stated.
CNN’s investigation raised questions about potential conflicts of interest between Kushner’s volunteer role as a peace envoy to the Middle East, and his firm’s financial investments. Kushner’s attorney did not address his client’s role as a negotiator on behalf of the Trump administration.
As part of the review into Kushner’s financial holdings, CNN used Israeli financial transparency laws to trace investments made by Phoenix Financial, a Tel Aviv-based firm that Kushner’s Affinity Partners doubled its stake in last year, shortly before Trump returned to the Oval Office. CNN’s reporting specifically excluded Phoenix’s investments through retirement accounts and focused on insurance holdings instead.
Those records, which include only some of Phoenix’s holdings, show Phoenix has invested hundreds of millions of dollars into Elbit Systems. Phoenix also holds stakes in at least eight other companies providing equipment for the Israeli military ranging from drones and warships to demolition machinery, CNN found.
All nine companies identified by CNN saw their stock value climb last year, with many stating the war in Gaza had driven demand for their businesses.
Affinity doesn’t directly hold a stake in the nine companies CNN identified – but it does stand to reap rewards when Phoenix makes a profit. Kushner described Phoenix as Affinity’s “best investment” in September 2025.
CNN found no indication that Kushner’s actions as a diplomat directly affected the investments reviewed. Kushner’s attorney told CNN his client has “never participated in or directed Phoenix’s decisions” on where to invest.
A day after CNN’s reporting, Kushner posted a rare response on X, calling CNN’s story “deeply misleading.” Kushner did not point to any inaccuracies in the piece in his post.
“Misleading stories will not distract me from the work President Trump asked me to do: help end wars, bring people together and pursue peace. That work is too important,” Kushner wrote on X.
Garcia referenced Kushner’s social media post, writing “despite your denial of improper behavior, the fact remains that you have been allowed to hold a position of enormous power and responsibility, exempt from financial disclosure requirements and outside oversight.”
In addition to CNN’s report, the New York Times published a story detailing additional “intermingling” between Kushner’s volunteer diplomatic role and his businesses, as it related to the war in Ukraine.
US talks with Russia to end that war have expanded to include a multibillion-dollar deal selling oil assets from one of Russia’s biggest energy companies to a group of investors with ties to Steve Witkoff and Kushner, the two main negotiators for the Trump administration, according to the Times.
A spokeswoman for Witkoff told the Times he “has no conflict of interest or financial stake in this matter” and said his work for the US administration is undertaken “at his own expense.”
Kushner’s attorney did not respond to CNN’s inquiry about this reporting.
Garcia and other Democrats have for years demanded answers from the White House and Trump’s family about concerns over “apparent influence peddling and quid pro quo deals” and whether foreign money is being used “to buy access to the President and influence American policy.”
In March, Garcia and Oregon Sen. Ron Wyden specifically requested information from the White House about Affinity Partners’ fundraising in the Middle East – Kushner secured a $2 billion investment for his firm from Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund in 2021— in light of Kushner’s government work.
Neither Kushner nor Affinity Partners responded to the congressmen’s earlier request.
The House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform is the main investigative committee in the House but the minority party requests from lawmakers on the committee are voluntary and can be ignored without legal consequences. Subpoenas can only be authorized by the committee chair or by committee vote. If the balance of power shifts as a result of the midterm elections in November, Democrats would be able to open an official investigation.
After Republicans won the House in 2023, the Oversight Committee, the Judiciary Committee and the Ways and Means Committee opened similar investigations into Hunter Biden’s business dealings overseas and alleged he was profiting from his father’s presidency.

articles.summary: ‘All I want to do is cry’: trauma of 7 October survivors three years after the attacks  The GuardianIsrael marks three years since Hamas-led 7 October 2023 attacks  BBCIsraelis mourn on the anniversary of the Oct. 7 attack as Palestinians grapple with war it sparked  The IndependentI documented the crimes of October 7. Too many still believe the lies of Hamas  The TelegraphHundreds attend October 7 vigil at Bondi, three years after terror attack &nbsp...
articles.full_text:
Keith Siegel spent many of his long hours in Hamas captivity in Gaza etching everything that happened after 7 October 2023 into his memory. For 484 days, he recited to himself every place he was held, the dates he was moved and every attack or humiliation he endured or witnessed.
He aimed to store intelligence that could help Israeli forces free other hostages if he was released, to keep track of time as the days slid by and be able to tell his family what happened to him. Now his body is free, but he cannot loosen those memories.
“I’m living a kind of dual life,” he said in an interview in Tel Aviv. “I’m here for some of the time, and I’m in Gaza some of time. It’s very challenging to convey in words what it was like.”
Siegel and his wife, Aviva, were among 251 people taken captive to Gaza on the deadliest day in Israel’s history, when Hamas militants broke across the border to launch a wave of attacks on kibbutzim, border towns, military bases and music festivals.
Israel’s security forces were caught by surprise, and by the time they regained control of the area, 1,209 people had been killed, the majority of them civilians, including 36 children, according to records kept by the Israeli newspaper Haaretz.
The cemetery at Nir Oz contains two lines of fresh headstones, marking lives that all ended on that same date. A shared plot for a family of five – a mother, father and their three young children – has been made into a garden with space left for their still-living grandparents.
Caretaker Shlomo Margalit, who will soon turn 89, points to the graves of three of his oldest friends, founding members of the kibbutz who came to Nir Oz from Haifa with him in the 1950s.
“This is my life project, as well as my home,” Margalit said, explaining why he has come back to a place of such loss. He is waiting for a new house but, for now, staying in the former home of Gadi Moses, 82, who survived 482 days as a hostage.
The graves he tends are a silent testament to the brutality of the attacks and the scale of the state’s failure, which in Nir Oz was staggering, even on a day of terrible failures.
A five-person volunteer defence force held Hamas at bay for at least two hours, Margalit said. When they had all been shot, the kibbutz was taken over and sacked, homes burned, families slaughtered and kidnapped.
Then, before the first Israeli soldier arrived, the Hamas forces, other Palestinian gunmen and civilian looters all left. Nir Oz had been forgotten by the army and ripped apart without the military firing a single shot to defend it.
In total, 47 people were killed and 76 taken to Gaza, including Shiri Bibas, her 10-month-old baby Kfir and four-year-old Ariel, who were killed in Gaza. The dead and hostages represented more than a quarter of the small community.
Revisiting that terrible day, and the trauma that followed, is painful and exhausting for Margalit, but he still accepts interviews for a simple reason. “I want people to know what really happened here,” the 89-year-old said.
The third anniversary of the 7 October attacks falls a few weeks before national elections, and much of the country is caught up in a furious debate about responsibility for the deadliest day in Israel’s history and the conduct of the war that followed.
Survivors and bereaved relatives are avoiding the political fray, still grappling with the trauma and the struggle to rebuild something like normality.
In Nir Oz, there is a terrible, almost irreconcilable struggle between re-establishing the kibbutz as a living community, and preserving physical testimony of the attack.
The cemetery echoes with the sound of construction and families have already moved into several rows of new houses near the kibbutz entrance.
But on the other side of the compound, paths still lead between blackened ruins and memorials to the dead. Some bereaved survivors want the homes of loved ones preserved this way as permanent monuments to mark their loss.
“There are families that can’t [bear to] live here, but want a memorial place to come to visit,” Margalit said. “On the other hand, can you build a new kibbutz where children grow up running around between burnt houses?”
He is on the remembrance committee and, two years on, they are struggling to reach a decision on this impossible choice. “Is there right or wrong here? No,” he said. “We are dealing with that, trying to find an answer.”
One compromise might be a memorial garden on the border of the kibbutz. For now, there are plaques with the stories of families attacked on that day and a memorial house to remember the dead and kidnapped.
When the kibbutz took a collective decision to return and rebuild, Margalit and his wife, Hanna, knew they wanted to join. His only concession to the trauma was asking for a new home that did not face Gaza.
“I’ve found myself building this place for the second time,” he said. “I know when I’m gone, I will have done something with my life. I took part in putting this spot on the map.”
The Siegels, who lived in the nearby kibbutz of Kfar Aza, also among the worst hit, have decided not to return as they focus on mental and physical recovery. Aviva was 62 when she was kidnapped. Keith was 64.
“What happened to me in Gaza, what happened with Keith in Gaza, it’s there all the time,” said Aviva.
“I understand that it’s going to be a process of healing. There’s always things that remind me, and if I don’t remember, then he reminds me. If I’m cooking lunch or making a cup of tea and I turn around and see Keith with tears in his eyes, because he just read something or let himself feel.”
The days approaching the anniversary have been particularly difficult, she said. Last year, at this time, she was still campaigning for the release of other hostages, her own emotions held at bay by the urgency of that campaign.
For a time, she tried to deal with the trauma by telling herself, over and over again “I must feel lucky,” simply because she had made it back alive.
Now she has allowed herself to feel again, and as 7 October approached, she has realised how raw the wounds still are. “Getting ready [for the anniversary] has been very very painful,” she said. “The last couple of weeks all I want to do is cry. Now I’m feeling things I didn’t feel before.”
“When I hear my grandson say he is afraid of being kidnapped in the middle of the night, it breaks my heart.”
She has written a book, Survived to Tell, about the ordeal, which she describes as therapy and an act of celebration. She wrote so her grandchildren could read about what she and Keith endured, for other hostages who couldn’t tell their own stories and to inspire a broader audience in Israel and beyond.
After the exhausting campaign to get Keith and other hostages home, she said she had struggled to concentrate on the election. Keith’s political focus is an independent inquiry into 7 October to prevent other families suffering as his has.
He said: “There needs to be an investigation to understand how this happened, in order to do everything possible that it won’t happen again. So many people were killed, injured, traumatised.”
Benjamin Netanyahu, the prime minister, has fiercely opposed an independent state commission of inquiry. Critics say he is afraid it would expose his own failings.
In the immediate aftermath of the attacks, few people inside or outside Israel expected him to stay in power long, particularly as the country’s coalition governments have rarely served out their full terms.
Netanyahu had for years championed a foreign and security policy based on the premise that Hamas was “contained” in Gaza, behind unbreachable layers of fortifications.
The security officials who were in command that day have all stepped down yet, three years on, Netanyahu is still in power, having deflected all demands for his resignation.
Yaakov Godo, a bereaved father, interrupted Netanyahu’s speech at the official commemoration event this year to accuse him of negligence.
“You did not protect my son on 7 October, you did not protect 1,200 people murdered in one day. Shame!” he shouted, before being ushered away.
Both US and Israeli officials have said Netanyahu rejected ceasefire deals that could have halted the war in Gaza and brought many Israeli hostages home sooner. But criticising the prime minister means venturing into a vicious political debate where age and loss offer little protection.
Yocheved Lifshitz, 88, was taken hostage from Nir Oz with her husband Oded, whose magnificent cactus garden blooms at the heart of the kibbutz. He died in Gaza, she survived and since her return she has been a vocal critic of Netanyahu.
A candidate for Netanyahu’s Likud party, Itzik Bonzel, said last month that he wished he could turn back the clock and return her to Hamas captivity. He later apologised, blaming grief for his son who died fighting in Gaza, but Lifshitz denounced it as a proxy attack driven by the prime minister.

articles.summary: AfD candidate elected speaker of German regional parliament for first time  BBCState parliament elects Germany’s first far-right speaker since second world war  The GuardianThe AfD’s dominance in Saxony-Anhalt  The EconomistGerman far right secures first regional parliament president  Financial TimesGermany news: Far-right AfD gets first house speaker in a German state parliament  DW.com
articles.full_text:
A month after Germany's far-right AfD scored a decisive victory in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, the party's candidate Tobias Rausch has been elected as parliament speaker there too.
Not since World War Two has a far-right party secured the post of speaker, and protesters outside the building in Magdeburg held up banners saying, "Never again is now".
Although the AfD fell three seats short of a majority in last month's election, Rausch, 35, comfortably won Tuesday's vote with the support of 9 MPs from other parties.
"The days of political firewalls should be a thing of the past," Rausch said after the vote, rejecting a post-war consensus in German politics not to work with the far right.
This was the first time since last month's state vote that Saxony-Anhalt's newly elected representatives had gathered in parliament, and regional Greens party leader Susan Sziborra-Seidlitz said "a line has been crossed" with the election of a far-right speaker of parliament, and it was a watershed moment.
"We will not let ourselves be intimidated, and we will not sit by when rights are curtailed either here or for people in the state," she said.
The AfD is considered pro-Russian and anti-immigrant, with plans to segregate child refugees in schools, as well as intolerant towards the LGBT community.
Within Saxony-Anhalt it is also classed as "right-wing extremist" by domestic intelligence, a description rejected by party leaders. Until now its members have sat on the right fringe of the state parliament, but ahead of Tuesday's inaugural session it successfully argued that it should now sit in the centre.
Rausch, a trained estate agent, has been a member of the parliament for 10 years and he is seen as a close confidant of local AfD leader Ulrich Siegmund, a charismatic figure who is now seeking to become state premier in December.
His new role is largely symbolic, but Rausch will now chair debates, have the power to control access to the parliament building and represent parliament at official events.
Although his victory was secured by five MPs from the hard-left BSW, there was surprise that four other unidentified MPs also voted for Rausch. Commentators immediately asked if he had secured the backing of members of the conservative CDU of Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who has ruled out working with the AfD.
Fourteen of the CDU's state MPs took part in the vote, but only five of them abstained as planned, and one unconfirmed report suggested four may have backed Rausch. Ahead of the vote, all 15 had ruled out voting for the AfD.
Outside parliament, more than 300 protesters voiced their anger at the AfD's victory, and they crowded around Ulrich Siegmund as he spoke to German media.
Siegmund's bid to become state premier is by no means secure. Like Rauch he will need the backing of 42 MPs in the 83-seat legislature.
The BSW has refused to enter into a coalition with the AfD and has said it would instead back a non-partisan candidate for state premier and abstain in December's vote.

articles.title: Yemen forces claim key gains near Bab al-Mandeb: What’s the latest? - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: Yemen forces claim key gains near Bab al-Mandeb: What’s the latest?  Al JazeeraIran war live: Yemen forces claim control over strategic Taiz mountain peak  Al JazeeraSaudi-backed forces run over surrendering Houthis with trucks  The TelegraphYemeni military says it has retaken Mokha and 'secured' Red Sea waterway  BBCYemeni government fighters shown driving vehicles over Houthi opponents  Reuters
articles.full_text:
Yemeni government forces say they have seized several strategic positions near the Bab al-Mandeb strait from the Iran-aligned Houthis, as fighting intensifies along the country’s western coast.
In response, the Houthis, an armed group also known by its Arabic name Ansar Allah, or Supporters of God, have claimed attacks on airports, oil infrastructure and military sites in Saudi Arabia.
The latest offensive by the Saudi-backed Yemeni government army follows major Houthi gains in September, when the group swept over the country’s Red Sea coast, capturing the strategic port city of Mocha and territory around the Bab al-Mandeb, one of the world’s most important shipping routes.
Rashad al-Alimi, chairman of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council, has said the government’s new operation – Dawn of Yemen – announced on Sunday, aims to retake all remaining Houthi-held territory, including the capital, Sanaa, which the group has controlled since 2014, when the war first started.
So, where does the fighting stand, and what could happen next?
What is the latest?
Southwestern Yemen has witnessed the heaviest fighting, particularly along the Red Sea coast and around Taiz.
Yemen’s government forces backed by Saudi Arabia said they, together with the Popular Resistance Forces, had taken control of the al-Manzara, al-Ashari and Dhiban mountains in Haifan, south of Taiz.
Earlier, Yemeni government forces claimed they had captured Mocha and Dhubab, both in Taiz governorate, as well as positions around Bab al-Mandeb, in a rapid Saudi-backed counteroffensive.
Government forces, supported by heavy Saudi air strikes, reached the outskirts of Mocha on Monday as Houthi fighters retreated towards the highlands, four government sources told the Reuters news agency.
Yemen’s Defence Ministry later said the city had fallen.
Without revealing any specifics, a Houthi military spokesman on Tuesday said the group remained in control of its battlefield gains and described reports from its opponents as “fabricated heroics”.
Al Jazeera has not independently verified the full extent of the government’s territorial gains.
Fernando Carvajal, a former United Nations Security Council adviser on Yemen, said the battle for Mocha will be key to the next phase of fighting.
“This will be a vital sign for us if the Yemeni government forces, led by the Southern Giants and other southern forces, can hold this city. Because, at the moment, when you look at the battle plan, Mocha is surrounded by Houthis from all three sides, and you have the Red Sea,” he told Al Jazeera.
“So, we need to wait just a little bit more to see if indeed the government forces can hold this city and then use it as a staging point to take on the Houthis on other fronts.”
The fighting has also extended northwards along the Red Sea coast to Hodeidah, which has been under Houthi control since October 2014. The Houthis had captured Sanaa weeks before that.
The Saudi-led coalition’s spokesman, Major-General Turki al-Maliki, said its naval forces struck Houthi “military targets” in the Hodeidah governorate, including weapons depots and facilities used to store explosive-laden boats and naval mines.
Al-Maliki said the operation “thwarted a planned attack” on waterways in the southern Red Sea. The coalition also said its naval forces had carried out a military operation in Hodeidah.
Meanwhile, the Houthis said their forces carried out dozens of strikes on Tuesday targeting “enemy” reinforcements east of al-Jawf governorate, resulting in an unspecified number of casualties.
The Houthis have simultaneously stepped up attacks on Saudi Arabia, according to Houthi-affiliated media. They targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, an Aramco refinery in Rabigh, Abha airport and the Khamis Mushait military base with missiles and drones, as well as sites in the southern Saudi cities of Najran and Jazan.
Saudi Arabia has yet to comment on all those specific claims.
However, on Tuesday, the Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation said the King Abdullah Bin Abdulaziz international airport in Jazan and the Najran international airport were targeted in two attacks on Monday evening, causing three minor injuries.
Later in the day, the Houthis claimed another attack on a Saudi airport, this time targeting Abha International Airport in Asir Province, with a ballistic missile.
Riyadh has yet to confirm the alleged attack.
What is the humanitarian situation on the ground?
The escalation is worsening what was already one of the world’s gravest humanitarian crises.
The International Organization for Migration said on Monday that more than 184,000 people have been displaced since the war resumed.
According to the World Health Organization, the latest fighting has killed at least 959 people and wounded more than 4,200.
The fighting has also disrupted healthcare in the war-devastated country.
“Yemen’s latest escalation is pushing an already fragile health system towards breaking point,” warned Annette Heinzelmann, WHO’s emergency director for the eastern Mediterranean region.
What is the international reaction?
The escalation has drawn a response from Saudi Arabia’s regional allies, with Turkiye and Pakistan agreeing to rapidly deploy military forces and capabilities to Saudi Arabia under the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement.
Signed in August, the pact is designed to strengthen collective deterrence and stipulates that an armed attack against Saudi Arabia, Pakistan or Turkiye will be regarded as an attack on all three.
The United States, one of Saudi Arabia’s closest allies, is providing intelligence support to Riyadh, according to media reports.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Monday Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government had “a right to defend themselves”.
“And obviously the Yemeni forces are going to try to retake territory that they were ousted from,” he told reporters.

Ethiopia’s Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has insisted that his landlocked country must have access to the Red Sea, even as neighbouring countries have said responsibility for the sea rests with the states along its shores.
Abiy made the demand as he was sworn in for another five-year term on Monday.
Repeating previous assertions, Abiy said in a speech in Parliament that the country would work to secure a port on the Red Sea, saying that access was critical to Ethiopia’s “civilisation”.
“Based on the principle of give and take, we will work diligently to ensure that Ethiopia has an outlet to the sea,” he said.
Ethiopia lost direct access to the Red Sea in 1993 after Eritrea, formerly a region of Ethiopia, became independent.
Abiy’s call came as Ethiopia’s relations with its neighbours have worsened in recent months, with Addis Ababa accusing Eritrea, Egypt and Sudan of supporting opposition forces in Tigray following a resurgence of the fighting against Abiy’s government in the northern region.
For its part, Eritrea has accused Ethiopia of seeking access to the sea through its territory. A separate dispute over Ethiopia’s Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam on the Nile River has strained relations with Egypt and Sudan, which rely on the river for water.
Four of the five countries bordering the Red Sea – Egypt, Eritrea, Sudan and Somalia – met on Sunday in Egypt’s New Alamein and called for cooperation on regional issues.
They said governance of the Red Sea was the exclusive responsibility of its coastal states and rejected actions that could affect Egypt and Sudan’s use of Nile waters.
The following day, Ethiopia’s Foreign Ministry said discussions over the Red Sea must account for the country’s “legitimate interests and enduring connection” to the body of water.
Somalia’s president, Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, who attended the Egypt summit, congratulated Abiy on his re-election.
“I look forward to working closely together to strengthen Somalia-Ethiopia relations & advance peace, stability & shared prosperity for our peoples & the Horn of Africa,” he said in a post on X.
Mohamud had previously told Al Jazeera that Somalia did not object to Ethiopia gaining access to the Red Sea through Somali territory but added that the two countries would need to officially negotiate.
Evariste Ndayishimiye, Burundi’s president, also wished Abiy “every success during his renewed mandate”. Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, the chairperson of the African Union Commission, also sent a message of congratulations.

Russian spies, and agents from other countries with feared intelligence services, have also been known to urinate in the toilets of diplomats and journalists to show they are capable of entering their homes.
In perhaps the most notorious example, the Wall Street Journal reported in 2023 that a Russian federal security service (FSB) agent defecated in the suitcase of a senior US official while he was visiting Russia.
Sarah Rainsford, the BBC’s former Russia correspondent, recalled in her memoir Goodbye to Russia that spies entered her flat and left “a large unflushed deposit in each toilet” as a calling card.
Luke Harding, a Guardian reporter, also claimed FSB officers would often break into his Moscow apartment, including once when agents left behind a sex manual, shortly before he was expelled from Russia in 2011.
US officials in 2014 reported that Soviet-era counterintelligence tactics were again being used against their diplomats, including tyre-slashing and multiple mysterious break-ins.
In some incidents, windows would be left open or personal belongings moved.
‘Operational psychology’
Michael McFaul, the former US ambassador to Russia, complained at the time of being followed almost everywhere and having his inbox hacked and phones tapped.
The strategy dates back to the Cold War of the 1960s when the KGB developed “operational psychology”, Mr Harding reported in his book Mafia State.
The Soviets were inspired by German Stasi agents, who would target the homes of dissidents to try to make them think they were going mad.
Officers would remove pictures from walls or swap one type of tea for another, leaving their targets largely unaware that the Stasi was behind the disturbances. In one particularly alarming incident, a vibrator was sent to a target’s wife.
Some victims suffered breakdowns or ended up killing themselves as a result.
Jürgen Fuchs, a writer who was targeted by the Stasi, described the “Zersetzung” technique as “an assault on the human soul”.
He was convinced before his death in 1999 that he had been deliberately exposed to radiation by the secret police, causing his terminal cancer, after three dissidents died within a short period from similar rare forms of leukaemia.

The European continent is experiencing the largest and most extensive rearmament phase since the post-World War II era. According to new analytical data published by the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI) and the NATO alliance, the total military expenditures of European countries are expected to reach 574 billion euros in 2026.
An analysis of the figures shows that just five years ago — in 2021 — the continent's defense budget stood at 283 billion euros, meaning the nominal volume of expenditures has increased by a staggering 103 percent over this short period.
Ratio to GDP and Comparative Dynamics with the US
The share of defense spending in the economy has also changed radically:
- Sharp increase in GDP share: While in 2021 military expenditures accounted for an average of 1.64 percent of Europe's gross domestic product (GDP), by the end of 2026 this figure rose to 2.55 percent;
- Infrastructure investments: In addition, member states are channeling another 1.4 percent of GDP into military infrastructure, logistics, and the strengthening of overall security;
- Faster growth rate than the US: Over the past five years, Europe has increased its military spending by a net 291 billion euros, doubling them. For comparison, over the same period, the US defense budget grew by 28 percent (199 billion euros in absolute terms).
Germany Leads, While the Baltics and Poland See Unprecedented Surges
By country, the largest financial changes on the continent are being observed in Germany:
- Berlin's 2.6-fold surge: Germany remains the clear leader in Europe in terms of total military expenditure volume. The country has increased its defense budget 2.6 times, raising it from 48 billion euros in 2021 to 125 billion euros in 2026;
- Eastern flank record: Growth has taken an even sharper pace in countries located on NATO's eastern borders. Poland has increased its military budget 3.5 times, Estonia 3.6 times, and Lithuania has already managed to increase it by a striking 4.3 times;
- 5% target achieved first: Poland and the Baltic states have practically achieved ahead of schedule the strategic milestone set at the 2025 NATO summit — the plan to bring defense spending to 5 percent of GDP by 2035.
Explosion in Military-Industrial Complex Revenues
The sharp increase in public procurement has also been clearly reflected in the financial turnover of leading defense corporations:
- European industry: The revenue of major European military-industrial companies with an annual turnover exceeding 1 billion euros grew from 104 billion euros in 2021 to 166 billion euros;
- US giants: Meanwhile, the revenue of US defense corporations expanded from 311 billion euros to 427 billion euros during the same period.
According to experts, the new rules adopted within NATO — the requirement to allocate 3.5 percent of GDP to core military needs, and 1.5 percent to cybersecurity, protection of critical infrastructure, and civil preparedness — will ensure the continuous adaptation of Europe's financial system toward defense in the coming decade.

General Alexus Grinkevich, Supreme Commander of NATO’s Allied Forces in Europe, is developing a strategy aimed at achieving a rapid and decisive victory should Russia launch an attack on NATO’s eastern border. This plan centers on the fusion of drones and artificial intelligence with conventional military units. Titled the “Theory of Victory,” the strategy is scheduled for unveiling on October 12 in Poland amidst escalating tensions between NATO and Russia.
The “Theory of Victory” document is publicly accessible and outlines NATO’s intended response to a potential Russian incursion. Colonel Martin O’Donnell, spokesperson for General Grinkevich, emphasized the alliance’s defensive stance and the importance of preventing unintended provocations. He stated:
“The Alliance is purely defensive.” – Colonel Martin O’Donnell
General Grinkevich’s strategy aims to swiftly incapacitate Russian forces by targeting their command and control systems, combining ground troops with advanced drone operations and AI capabilities.
NATO’s Preparedness for Emerging Threats
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte has noted that there are currently no signs of Russia preparing for a conventional attack on the alliance. However, he warned of ongoing hybrid warfare threats requiring sustained vigilance. Ahead of the strategy’s release, European NATO members have significantly increased their defense budgets, though disagreements remain over prioritizing traditional armaments versus cutting-edge technology.
- Conventional weaponry
- Advanced technological systems
The United States is also deeply involved in these efforts. In summer 2023, Washington circulated a survey among NATO partners concerning defense expenditures, aiming to inform decisions about potentially reducing American military presence in Europe. This questionnaire also explored allies’ willingness to contribute additional forces to support General Grinkevich’s defense plans. The full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022 has been a catalyst for accelerating NATO’s strategic innovations.
The introduction of the “Theory of Victory” represents a significant milestone in NATO’s adaptation to evolving global security challenges. By integrating innovative tools like drones and artificial intelligence, the alliance seeks to maintain a technological edge that could fundamentally influence future combat scenarios. This strategy also addresses the persistent hybrid threats that continue to endanger the security of NATO member states.
As NATO prepares to unveil its new strategy, understanding the intricate blend of advanced tactics involving drones and AI becomes essential. This approach not only highlights the alliance’s commitment to rapid defense but also reflects a significant shift in military operations aimed at countering potential threats from Russia.

Hrynkevych will present a strategy for rapidly repelling a Russian attack in Poland. NATO plans to combine traditional forces with drones and AI.
NATO’s top military commander is working on a strategy to achieve a swift victory against a Russian attack on the alliance’s eastern flank, with a particular focus on integrating new defense technologies, such as drones and artificial intelligence, into traditional defense. Bloomberg reported, UNN writes.
Details
The document, titled "Theory of Victory," which the publication reviewed in an unclassified form, will be presented by NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe, General Alexus Grynkewich, in Poland on October 12, amid heightened tensions between NATO and Russia.
According to senior officials and diplomats familiar with the matter, it aims to clarify how the alliance would respond to a possible invasion of NATO territory. There have recently been numerous reports that Moscow is considering such actions, the publication writes.
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte recently said there were no signs that Russia was preparing for a conventional attack on the alliance, but Europe must be prepared for sustained hybrid attacks.
Grynkewich’s spokesperson, Colonel Martin O’Donnell, declined to discuss the plan’s details but emphasized that the alliance is "purely defensive."
"The Supreme Allied Commander Europe’s ‘Theory of Victory’ is simple: preserve NATO’s advantage," O’Donnell said. "Given the unstable and complex global security situation, we need to create the conditions now to deter aggression and, if necessary, prevail in the event of an attack."
Although the general principles of NATO’s approach to warfare are known, open discussion of them is rare, the publication notes. The initiative is intended to reassure the public about NATO’s readiness while also presenting a more concrete picture of what lies behind increased defense spending.
The document also aims to illustrate to allies how NATO will integrate conventional weapons with new capabilities that have emerged since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, as well as call for increased investment in defense and better preparedness, sources said.
The strategy insists on NATO’s defensive nature and avoiding unintended provocations, while clearly mentioning the need for collective action against hybrid threats – aggressive actions below the threshold of conflict – as part of deterrence. By demonstrating readiness, NATO wants the adversary to conclude that it cannot win, the strategy says.
"But if NATO were attacked, it would block the invasion through a combination of ground forces and other resources from NATO’s Eastern Flank Deterrence Initiative, a concept based on low-cost unmanned vehicles, minimally crewed systems, and artificial-intelligence-based targeting. Once it had freedom of maneuver, it would seek to destroy enemy command and control in order to achieve a rapid and overwhelming defeat of Russian forces," the publication says.
NATO allies, particularly in Europe, have significantly increased defense spending, and tensions have arisen over how to prioritize conventional weapons, such as tanks, versus alternative technologies that have come to the forefront in the war in Ukraine, the publication writes.
This summer, the United States sent NATO allies a questionnaire assessing their defense spending and support for the policies of U.S. President Donald Trump, in order to inform decisions on a planned reduction in U.S. military assets allocated to the defense of Europe.
As part of the questionnaire, the United States asked whether the allies still had forces that could be made available to NATO for Grynkewich’s defense plans, the publication notes.

British intelligence agencies are investigating whether their classified information or spies were compromised in the biggest espionage scandal in modern German history.
August Hanning – the former head of Germany’s foreign intelligence service – and a senior official at the agency, named only as Manfred D, were arrested on Tuesday on suspicion of espionage and treason.
Mr Hanning is accused of illegally collecting classified documents for 16 years through Manfred D and selling some secrets to a foreign power.
German security sources said some of the high-level information the pair handled came from partner intelligence agencies abroad, raising the prospect that British and US intelligence had been compromised.
It has also raised fears that US and British human sources, either agents or informants operating in the field, could be identified through information that has been shared.
The scandal has shocked the Western intelligence community, with sources describing the alleged breach as a major coup for a foreign power and potentially deeply damaging to the Western intelligence-sharing alliance.
MI6 and GCHQ, as well as several US agencies, are now believed to be undergoing a systematic internal review of all sensitive information shared with European allies during the relevant period.
The Telegraph understands that their primary focus is safeguarding sources who may have been put at risk by the alleged leak. Similar audits are likely to be undertaken by all Germany’s intelligence-sharing partners and allies.
